Iran government pushes talks line, but power lies elsewhere. Amid threats of war and mounting fears of economic collapse, Iran's government is seeking to reinforce its case for moderation in a fractured and deeply polarized political landscape.

Netanyahu backs pressure-first strategy on Iran after Trump talks. Israel wants to intensify economic pressure on Iran while preserving the threat of military action, a senior Israeli official said after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's meeting with US President Donald Trump.

Tehran tests a more confrontational strategy. Iran's ballistic missile strike on US forces in Jordan and its seizure of three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have dealt a fresh blow to efforts to preserve last month's Iran-US understanding.

Trump likely to expand strikes on Iran rather than withdraw, ex-Pentagon official says. US President Donald Trump's most likely response to the conflict with Iran will be to intensify air strikes against a broader range of targets rather than withdraw or launch a ground invasion, former senior Pentagon official David Des Roches told Iran International TV.

Iranian agents cut protester's royalist tattoos before killing him. Iranian security agents allegedly cut away skin bearing tattoos of Reza Shah and an imperial crown before killing a 21-year-old protester before later shooting him dead, according to sources close to his family.

Tehran uses war as cover to ramp up executions, political prisoners say. Three prominent political prisoners held in Tehran's Evin prison issued a joint statement accusing the establishment of using regional war as a cover to escalate domestic repression and attempt to rebuild its lost authority through executions.

From cafes to buskers, Tehran tightens its grip on the fabric of everyday life. In the quiet hours of Wednesday morning, municipal crews swept through Sanaei Street in central Tehran with sledgehammers, reducing sidewalk planters, benches, and concrete borders outside local cafes to rubble.

State TV dispute exposes limits of oversight in Iran. Iran's state broadcaster has ignored a formal order from its own watchdog to stop censoring senior officials, highlighting the gap between the country's formal institutions and where authority is exercised in practice.

'Western trap': calls for restraint grow in Tehran after Ukraine attack. Signs of reluctance to widen the conflict are emerging in Tehran, with conservative politicians and media urging restraint even as they accuse the United States and Israel of orchestrating Ukraine's attack on an Iranian vessel.

Where steak is a dream. A social media exchange about steak struck a chord among Iranian users this week, turning one young user's dream into a broader conversation about economic hardship and political frustration.

US offers $15 million reward over IRGC drone network. The United States has offered a reward of up to $15 million for information that disrupts the financial mechanisms of Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), focusing on a company Washington says plays a key role in producing drones used by Tehran and its regional allies.

UK charges man accused of spying on RAF base for Iran's IRGC. A dual British and Azerbaijani national has been arrested in Cyprus on suspicion of carrying out hostile surveillance for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in the first overseas investigation under Britain's National Security Act.

Tehran prosecutor takes legal action against opponents of executions. Tehran's prosecutor has launched legal action against an unspecified number of people for opposing the execution of detainees arrested during the January protests and defendants convicted in cases linked to the recent war, Iran's judiciary news outlet Mizan reported on Thursday.

Iran gambling network helped channel $4 billion through crypto exchange - Reuters. An illicit Iranian gambling network helped move at least $4 billion through an unlicensed Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange that also handled funds for sanctioned Iranian institutions, a Reuters investigation found.

Security forces seized Iran hospital, sent wounded protesters to morgue. Iranian security forces took control of a hospital in the western city of Khorramabad during January's nationwide crackdown, according to medical staff, transferring dozens of critically wounded protesters to the morgue instead of receiving further treatment.

Why Iran's leaders failed to see this generation coming. A gathering of thousands of teenagers at a Tehran mall to meet a popular YouTuber exposed a widening blind spot in Iran, some sociologists suggested: a generation whose values, social lives and sources of authority increasingly lie beyond the state's understanding.

US tightens military and financial pressure as Iran talks falter. The Trump administration on Friday outlined military and financial measures against Tehran alongside negotiations that President Donald Trump said were being undermined by Iran’s conduct.

Iran's hangings are 'murders,' says former UN prosecutor. Iran's latest wave of public hangings of protesters amounts to "killings" and "murders" that form part of a continuing crime against humanity, former United Nations prosecutor Professor Payam Akhavan told Iran International's Eye for Iran.

Ghalibaf reveals Tehran feared street unrest after Iran International broke Khamenei news. Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said authorities rushed to announce Ali Khamenei’s death and call supporters onto the streets after “overseas media” broke the news, fearing the situation on the streets could otherwise “take a completely different turn.”

Iran executes 20-year-old protester as fears grow for other detainees. Iranian authorities executed 20-year-old protester Arvin Kheirkhah at Shahroud prison on Saturday morning, according to information obtained by Iran International, amid concerns that several other detainees could also face execution.

China helps Iran chip away at US air superiority despite Xi’s no-arms pledge. Xi Jinping’s promise to Donald Trump that China would not arm Iran is being tested by Tehran’s alleged pursuit of Chinese MANPADS, relatively cheap weapons that could make future US and Israeli air campaigns more dangerous and expensive.

Iran ramps up threats to Mideast energy sites as fears of major US strike grow. Iranian officials on Saturday responded to reports of a possible large-scale US attack with threats to strike Israel and regional energy infrastructure, as public anxiety grows and motorists form long queues at gas stations.

Diplomatic window reopens as shadow of Iran war lingers. Diplomatic efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz accelerated on Sunday after US President Donald Trump called off a planned attack on Iran, with Tehran saying negotiations with Oman were nearing completion and mediators outlining a proposal to revive US-Iran talks.

More Iranian teenagers at risk of execution, rights groups warn. Rights groups have warned that more teenagers arrested during Iran's January uprising face imminent execution, saying authorities have intensified the use of death sentences against minors as part of a broader execution campaign.

Castel : la bataille se poursuit entre Gregory Clerc et la fille du fondateur. Une décision de la justice à Singapour rendue ce 30 juillet relance le bras de fer au long cours entre le directeur général de Castel et une partie des héritiers du fondateur Pierre Castel.

Ethiopian Airlines : une croissance forte mais pas assez d’avions, le paradoxe du leader africain de l’aérien. Avec 9,1 milliards de dollars de revenus, Ethiopian Airlines signe sa meilleure année. Mais les coûts à la hausse, sa flotte sous tension et une marge nette africaine en forte chute nuancent ce résultat.

RDC-Rwanda : ce que l’on sait du projet controversé de démobilisation des FDLR. Le gouvernement congolais a présenté un protocole d’accord qui ouvre la voie à la dissolution du groupe fondé par d’anciens génocidaires hutu rwandais. Kinshasa y voit une avancée majeure, tandis que Kigali dénonce une manipulation.

Le premier Sénat du Bénin entre en fonction. Instaurée par la révision constitutionnelle de novembre 2025, la première Chambre haute du pays est composée de 25 parlementaires. Reste à désigner son siège et surtout, son président.

Cameroun : pourquoi les accusations du capitaine Effoudou contre Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh créent le scandale. Déserteur et visé par un mandat d’arrêt pour escroquerie, l’ancien chef du bureau de renseignement de l’état-major de Paul Biya brise le silence depuis l’Europe. Ses accusations visant le secrétaire général de la présidence secouent Yaoundé.

Fintech : le régulateur de la Cemac en mission pour assainir le paiement électronique. Avec 3,74 milliards de transactions en 2024, le paiement mobile domine largement les échanges financiers en Afrique centrale. Le régulateur prépare un cadre inédit qui va remodeler le marché afin de mieux le contrôler.

Maroc-Espagne : afflux de migrants à Ceuta, neuf morts. Des centaines de personnes ont convergé dans la soirée du 30 juillet dans le nord du Maroc vers l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta. Plusieurs milliers de migrants y sont entrés ces derniers jours et neuf sont morts en tentant de la rejoindre à la nage.

À Pékin, les confidences des diplomates chinois sur le Maroc. Dix ans après la signature du partenariat stratégique entre les deux pays, Rabat continue d’occuper une place singulière dans la stratégie chinoise envers « le Sud global ».

Djibril Ouattara : « La Côte d’Ivoire s’inspire de l’Estonie pour développer ses infrastructures numériques publiques ». Le ministre ivoirien de la Transition numérique et de l’Innovation technologique veut porter la contribution de son secteur de 6 % à 15 % du PIB à l’horizon 2030. Et compte tout mettre en œuvre pour y parvenir. Entretien.

À l’ONU, un premier « vote indicatif » décevant pour Macky Sall. Si tout n’est pas encore joué, le premier scrutin secret visant à désigner le prochain secrétaire général de l’Organisation des Nations unies dessine une tendance défavorable aux deux candidats africains, dont Macky Sall.

Guerre au Soudan : les Boeing d’un contractant américain et l’étrange pont aérien vers les FSR. Une enquête de Reuters et un projet de rapport de l’ONU révèlent un pont aérien clandestin au profit des FSR d’Hemetti, qui aurait été opéré en partie depuis le Tchad. L’affaire ravive les soupçons sur le soutien des Émirats arabes unis aux paramilitaires soudanais.

Algérie-France : pourquoi Abdelmadjid Tebboune refuse toujours de parler à Emmanuel Macron. Deux ans après le soutien de Paris à la souveraineté marocaine sur le Sahara occidental, le président algérien n’a toujours pas pardonné à son ami français ce qu’il considère comme une trahison. Une rupture personnelle qui hypothèque l’ensemble de la relation franco-algérienne.

Afreximbank : les raisons de son retour au dollar. Après cinq ans d’émissions en yens et en yuans, la banque renoue avec le dollar en levant 1,5 milliard. Derrière ce grand retour se cachent une notation retrouvée et un pari calculé sur le calendrier.

Blocs pétroliers au Nigeria : la NNPC et Tony Elumelu recalés au profit de sociétés plus confidentielles. Le plus grand cycle d’octroi de licences du Nigeria depuis l’entrée en vigueur de la nouvelle loi pétrolière en 2021 a vu plusieurs producteurs pétroliers et gaziers établis repartir les mains vides.

Maroc : la crise au Moyen-Orient, point de bascule pour OCP ?. Le champion marocain des engrais sort d’une période de turbulences provoquée par le blocage du détroit d’Ormuz. Dans un décryptage vidéo, Jeune Afrique revient sur l’impact de cette épreuve pour le groupe et son patron, Mostafa Terrab.

Football en Côte d’Ivoire : l’accord secret qui a écarté Malick Tohé de la course à la tête de la FIF. Le vice-président de la « fédé » ivoirienne ne défiera pas son patron, Yacine Idriss Diallo. En échange, ce dernier lui a fait plusieurs concessions. Coulisses.

RDC : Katebe Katoto, frère de Katumbi et émissaire de Tshisekedi dans le Haut-Katanga. Alors que Félix Tshisekedi est en visite dans le Katanga, Raphaël Katebe Katoto y organise des consultations pour le compte du chef de l’État. Le demi-frère de l’opposant en exil Moïse Katumbi fait-il pour autant campagne pour le changement de Constitution voulu par le président ?

Affaire Zogo au Cameroun : ce qu’il faut retenir des déclarations du colonel Otoulou. L’audition de Jean-Pierre Otoulou, chef de la commission mixte ayant enquêté sur la mort de Martinez Zogo, se poursuit ces 3 et 4 août au tribunal militaire de Yaoundé. Jeune Afrique résume ses précédents passages à la barre.

Paul Biya toujours en Suisse, Ibrahim Traoré serre la vis, Fouzi Lekjaâ rebat les cartes… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur le séjour prolongé de Paul Biya en Suisse, analyse le durcissement de la politique religieuse d’Ibrahim Traoré au Burkina Faso, dresse le portrait du nouveau patron de Petrosen au Sénégal, décrypte le coup politique de Fouzi Lekjaâ au Maroc et s’interroge sur les critiques visant la Cour pénale internationale, accusée de cibler l’Afrique.

Ce discours de Hassan II que la Chine n’a jamais oublié. Une minute qui dure depuis des décennies. Alors que la Chine et le Maroc célèbrent les dix ans de leur « partenariat stratégique », le discours de 1960 de celui qui n’était encore que Moulay Hassan, à la tribune de l’ONU, continue d’éclairer les relations sino-marocaines.

Dangote peut-il remporter son pari de méga raffinerie au Kenya ?. Dangote ambitionne de faire du Kenya le pôle de raffinage de l’Afrique de l’Est avec un investissement de 17 milliards de dollars. Pour cela, il lui faut régler la question du financement, de l’approvisionnement et de la fiscalité… entre autres.

Homosexualité, guerre au Sahel et sécurité alimentaire : le best-of de nos infographies. Jeune Afrique a fait parler les chiffres et les cartes et vous propose cinq façons de voir autrement, pour mieux comprendre certaines évolutions majeures du continent.

Afflux de migrants à Ceuta : l’Espagne réclame une réunion européenne d’urgence. Madrid estime que la situation dans l’enclave est « quasiment » revenue à la normale après le retour au Maroc de « presque » tous les migrants arrivés ces derniers jours, au cœur d’une crise migratoire qui s’est muée en querelle diplomatique au sein de l’Union européenne.

Au Mali, l’ancien Premier ministre Moussa Mara a été libéré. Le président du parti Yelema, arrêté et écroué le 1er août 2025, a purgé sa peine d’un an de prison ferme consécutive à une condamnation pour « atteinte au crédit de l’État et opposition à l’autorité légitime ».

En Côte d’Ivoire, le RHDP ou l’épopée d’une machine politique. En deux décennies, le RHDP s’est transformé en une puissante machine politique qui domine la Côte d’Ivoire. Dans la Semaine de Jeune Afrique sur RFI, retour sur l’épopée d’une formation née dans l’opposition, forgée par les crises et portée au sommet par Alassane Ouattara.

De Pékin à Rabat, le soft power chinois joue la carte africaine. Échanges universitaires, visibilité dans les médias, soutien au développement de l’IA… La Chine veut que son influence culturelle soit à la hauteur de sa place de deuxième puissance économique mondiale. Et le Maroc s’impose comme l’un des principaux points d’ancrage de cette priorité stratégique sur le continent africain.

Cameroun : le réseau politico-business de Franck Biya, « candidat favori » à la vice-présidence. Homme d’affaires devenu prétendant à la succession de son père, Franck Biya tisse patiemment sa toile. De la famille aux cercles d’affaires, du palais d’Etoudi aux élites du Grand Nord en passant par les stars du sport, cartographie d’un réseau.

Du PNDS à la junte : au Niger, les routes de la drogue restent grandes ouvertes. Aux frontières du Mali, de l’Algérie et de la Libye, le Niger reste un pays de transit idéal pour les drogues qui voyagent des ports du golfe de Guinée aux marchés européens. Si l’ancien parrain Chérif Ould Abidine est décédé, d’ex-lieutenants ont pris le relais, avec la complicité récente de personnalités liées à la junte.

Au Cameroun, qui sont les défenseurs zélés de Paul Biya pendant son absence ?. Absent du Cameroun depuis le 7 juin, Paul Biya séjourne encore en Suisse. Certains ministres, parlementaires ou militants du RDPC rivalisent de formules lénifiantes. Pendant ce temps, d’autres poids lourds du régime se taisent.

Maroc-Chine : quel est le véritable poids de Pékin dans l’économie marocaine ?. Le Maroc occupe aujourd’hui une place de choix dans le déploiement industriel chinois, qui vise à pénétrer les marchés d’Europe et d’Afrique. Dix ans après la signature d’un partenariat stratégique entre Pékin et Rabat, JA fait le point.

Ceuta : l’Espagne dénonce une « attaque » contre « son intégrité territoriale ». Le premier ministre espagnol, Pedro Sanchez, qui s’est rendu sur place dans une ambiance électrique, s’est attaqué à des rumeurs lancées par des « mafias de trafiquants d’êtres humains », les accusant d’être à l’origine de cet afflux.

Quand le gouvernement américain publie une carte fantaisiste de l’Afrique. Lors d’une conférence internationale sur le sida, au Brésil, fin juillet, le département d’Etat a présenté une carte de l’Afrique où la Côte d’Ivoire s’est retrouvée dans le sud du continent et le Nigeria enclavé dans le Sahara. Le Cameroun, quant à lui, est devenu un Etat fantôme.

Remis en liberté, le rappeur et cinéaste marocain Mehdi Black Wind espère retrouver son autre port d’attache, Marseille. Artiste touche-à-tout et engagé contre les inégalités dans son pays, le Maroc, Mehdi Black Wind, de son vrai nom El Mahdi Lyoubi, avait été arrêté le 10 juillet sur sa terre natale. Son interpellation avait suscité un vaste élan de mobilisation.

Mohammed VI célèbre son règne en pleine crise migratoire avec l’Espagne. Environ 50 000 personnes ont rejoint clandestinement l’enclave espagnole, jeudi. Un nombre record, alors que le roi du Maroc fête ses vingt-sept ans sur le trône.

« C’était la chance de notre vie » : après un exil de seulement quelques heures à Ceuta, des dizaines de milliers de jeunes regagnent le Maroc. Encouragées par des messages sur les réseaux sociaux, quelque 50 000 personnes ont rejoint illégalement l’enclave espagnole depuis jeudi 30 juillet, un afflux sans précédent. Mais la plupart d’entre elles ont déjà été contraintes de faire le chemin retour.

Crise migratoire à Ceuta : retrouvez nos informations sur l’afflux de migrants dans l’enclave espagnole. Pedro Sanchez a réclamé une réunion des ministres de l’intérieur européens, tandis que le ministre de l’intérieur de l’Espagne a affirmé qu’« en moins de quarante-huit heures, la situation à Ceuta n’a[vait] plus rien à voir ». La plupart des 50 000 migrants entrés illégalement dans l’enclave espagnole sont retournés au Maroc.

En Libye, les manifestations contre les coupures électriques fragilisent le pouvoir à Tripoli. Plusieurs villes de l’Ouest libyen sont touchées par des manifestations provoquées par les coupures de courant. A Tripoli, certains habitants ont lancé un mouvement de désobéissance civile et demandent la démission du gouvernement.

Ceuta : l’UE convoque une réunion d’urgence afin d’échanger sur la crise migratoire. Des dizaines de milliers de migrants ont pénétré illégalement ces derniers jours dans l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta en provenance du Maroc. L’Espagne a affirmé, samedi, que la plupart des migrants étaient rentrés au Maroc, le premier ministre espagnol, Pedro Sanchez, dénonçant l’attitude « égoïste » de certains pays de l’UE.

Comment la canicule a mis la Tunisie sous tension ? Comprendre en trois minutes. Alors qu’une canicule étouffante affecte le réseau électrique du pays, des milliers de Tunisiens sont descendus dans la rue pour dénoncer l’inaction et la dérive autoritaire du pouvoir.

A Fnideq, près de Ceuta, la désillusion des jeunes Marocains après une traversée éclair en Europe. Alors que 50 000 personnes, de jeunes Marocains pour l’essentiel, se ruaient sur l’enclave espagnole, jeudi et vendredi, Ceuta est désormais désertée, la plupart des candidats à l’exil ayant fait demi-tour.

Immigration en Europe : quelle place Ceuta et Melilla occupent-elles ?. Si l’Espagne fait partie des principaux pays d’entrée dans l’Union européenne, aux côtés de la Grèce et de l’Italie, les flux arrivant dans ses deux enclaves du continent africain sont comparables à ceux d’autres routes.

Ceuta : au moins 72 personnes sont mortes en voulant rejoindre l’enclave espagnole, selon les autorités locales ; le Maroc fait état de 11 décès. L’Association marocaine des droits humains a fait état de « près de 130 victimes » et de dizaines de disparus, et appelé à l’ouverture d’une enquête indépendante sur les causes de cet afflux inédit de migrants. Le Maroc dénonce « l’exploitation malveillante » des réseaux sociaux et « la diffusion d’informations trompeuses » pour expliquer cette crise.

Felwine Sarr, écrivain : « Les budgets des nations africaines pourraient être orientés vers la dignité ». Dans un nouvel essai, « La Fabrique du présent », l’auteur sénégalais réfléchit à ce qui pourrait permettre l’essor en Afrique de sociétés davantage tournées vers la dignité de chacun. Il est nécessaire, explique-t-il dans un entretien au « Monde », de repenser les politiques publiques et de les redéfinir en fonction des philosophies et des ressources locales.

VIDÉO. « Je préfère mourir ici que de repartir » : quelques migrants entrés à Ceuta illégalement tentent de rester en Espagne. Après la ruée de migrants vers ce territoire espagnol, les autorités espagnoles dénombrent au moins 72 morts, principalement par noyade.

« Les gens viennent ici pour se reposer. Mais il devient très difficile de leur offrir cette sérénité » : en Tunisie, le secteur du tourisme affecté par les coupures d’électricité et d’eau à répétition. Le pays est confronté à des chaleurs exceptionnelles qui mettent à rude épreuve les réseau d’approvisionnement. Avec de lourdes conséquences pour les hôteliers et les restaurateurs, en pleine saison estivale.

Abdul Samad Rabiu, l’autre industriel multimilliardaire qui veut changer le Nigeria. « Fortunes africaines ». Son parcours rappelle celui d’Aliko Dangote, première fortune d’Afrique. Plus discret, le patron du groupe BUA a lui aussi bâti un empire dans le ciment et le sucre. Et lui aussi est originaire de Kano, carrefour millénaire du commerce transsaharien.

Soudan : une ONG accuse l’armée d’avoir tué 35 personnes dans une frappe de drone sur un tribunal du Darfour. Le conflit entre l’armée et les Forces de soutien rapide, qui a éclaté en 2023, a fait des dizaines de milliers de morts, provoqué le déplacement de millions de personnes et déclenché ce que les Nations unies décrivent comme la plus grave crise de la faim au monde.

Comment le Maroc met sous pression les enclaves espagnoles de Ceuta et de Melilla. L’arrivée soudaine de 50 000 personnes à Ceuta interroge sur le rôle de Rabat dans cette crise migratoire, alors que le royaume chérifien conteste l’appartenance des deux cités à l’Espagne.

A Ceuta, les habitants entre colère, angoisse et compassion. Deux jours après que l’enclave a vu affluer 50 000 personnes depuis la frontière marocaine, la cité a retrouvé son calme, dimanche, mais les habitants disent s’être sentis abandonnés par Madrid.

Des Etats africains sommés par les Etats-Unis de quitter la CPI. L’administration de Donald Trump a annoncé à la mi-juillet une guerre totale contre la Cour pénale internationale, établie à La Haye, alors que le pays n’en a jamais été membre.

Palestinian ‘doctor of the poor’ says he faces abuse, medical neglect in Israeli prison Submitted by Bilge Kotan on Sun, 08/02/2026 - 19:37 The 71-year-old physician, well known for providing care to low-income Palestinians, was arrested in the occupied West Bank in June News of Rantisi’s detention prompted widespread condemnation (Screengrab/X/@Mistaclim) Off Dr Mazen Rantisi, a 71-year-old Palestinian physician popularly described as the “doctor of the poor”, says he has suffered physical abuse and medical neglect since Israeli authorities detained him more than a month ago, Haaretz reported on Sunday. The doctor, known for often waiving fees, supplying medicines and operating a clinic that serves as a refuge for low-income Palestinians, was detained in a pre-dawn raid on his home in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank on 21 June. Prosecutors later indicted him for serving as chairman of the board of the Union of Health Work Committees, a Palestinian non-profit that provides medical care to thousands of Palestinians each year. According to the report, Rantisi told a lawyer from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel that prison authorities withheld his regular medication for the first 10 days in Ofer prison and are still denying him one of his medicines. His requests to see a doctor went unanswered, and a medic checked his pulse only once through a small opening in the cell door. Rantisi also reported physical violence, saying that said the prison units raided his cell several times a week and beat detainees. “The younger prisoners surround me to protect me, taking the beatings themselves,” Rantisi said, adding that the guards sprayed tear gas into the cell during one raid, leaving him struggling to breathe. Saja Mishraki-Baransa, the first lawyer to see Rantisi face to face since his arrest, said the physician has rapidly lost weight after receiving tiny portions of food that he described as unfit for human consumption, including mouldy bread, almost-rotten tomatoes, uncooked hummus and foul-smelling rice. The Israel Prison Service rejected the physician’s account, saying that it held all prisoners in accordance with the law, the Haaretz report said. The physician’s account, however, echoes accounts from other Palestinian detainees and prisoners. HEALTH: UNCOVERING WHY BABIES DIE. Field teams actively track children under five years of age every three months to closely observe health trajectories and vital events. Expectant mothers within the target areas are systematically registered and followed up with | AKU & CHAMPS programme At first glance, the Changan Karvaan parked outside one of Aga Khan University’s (AKU) field sites in Karachi’s Bhains Colony looks like an ordinary white minivan. Boxy, tinted windows, no markings to set it apart. It’s only when you get in that the disinfectant and medical equipment give it away. Under the bright clinical lights, you will find surgical gloves, syringes, tissue covers… everything needed to perform MITS, or minimally invasive tissue sampling, on even the smallest of babies in the localities of Ali Akbar Shah, Ibrahim Hyderi and Bhains Colony. This unusual approach to forensics has helped researchers paint one of the clearest pictures yet of why these babies die before their fifth birthday. In three of Karachi’s poorest neighbourhoods, a minimally invasive autopsy technique is doing what verbal accounts and hospital records couldn’t: naming the exact cause of death in babies before age five WHAT IS MITS In 2015, the Gates Foundation launched the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance (CHAMPS) programme to better understand why babies and young children die in poor countries. It was coordinated by University of Texas, Southwestern Medical Centre and aimed to combine clinical records, laboratory testing, verbal autopsies and, where families consent, MITS, to pinpoint the biological causes of stillbirths and deaths among children under five. MITS is a post-mortem exam in which tiny amounts of tissue and fluid from key organs are taken using fine needles. These samples are analysed for pathogens, infectious disease and malignant tumours. The results reveal the exact cause of death without a full surgical autopsy. The goal is to arm governments and health agencies with evidence, so they can tackle preventable child deaths. “Children die because of certain reasons — there’s intrauterine deaths, which are before birth,” says Dr Asim Beg, parasitologist at AKU who specialises in vector-borne diseases. “The real cause for those is also more speculative because, in Pakistan, a Muslim country, they don’t do post-mortems normally,” he tells Eos. The study operates across nine countries on two continents, but Pakistan posed an obstacle unique to it: a widespread religious conviction that invasive sampling would disrespect the dead. It took at least 28 fatwas [religious edicts], countless meetings and debates with local leaders, and deep community involvement before families started to consent. “When the surveillance team first approached families, the response was overwhelmingly negative,” says Sajid Abbas, a research manager for the study. “At least 60 to 70 per cent of households refused outright.” The data collected from a MITS sample is just as comprehensive as what you’d get from a full open autopsy, according to Dr Momin Kazi, the study’s lead researcher. Tissue is collected from the brain, heart, lungs and kidneys, and, for stillbirths, the placenta is taken in its entirety. Organ samples are obtained through a puncture no larger than a pen’s tip, alongside cerebrospinal fluid, nasal, rectal and stool swabs, plus biometric measurements and photographs. MITS identifies the cause of death in 98 to 100 per cent of cases, researchers say, because they draw on polymerase chain reactions (PCRs), chromatography, and every other test available. That level of accuracy is possible because findings are deliberated upon by a panel of 12-13 experts, including professors, government representatives and specialists from private hospitals. They systematically eliminate possibilities to find the cause. Often, the visible symptoms were the ones already treated, but an underlying condition went undetected, with no symptoms. The sample size isn’t yet enough for policy, researchers say, but MITS has revealed unprecedented detail: exact pathogens, hidden causes beneath treated symptoms and new local strains no other method would catch. Researchers deliberately chose this stretch of Karachi’s coastline as a study site because it functions as a “mini Pakistan”, with families from all linguistic backgrounds and faiths. RACE AGAINST TIME When a stillbirth occurs or a child under five dies, burial usually happens within two to four hours — arrangements are minimal, beyond a ghusl [ritual bath] and shrouding. Many such deaths happen at home and are rarely logged with a hospital, leaving the cause unknown. The team’s challenge was to even find out about these mortalities. “It’s not as if every death comes through a hospital,” says Abbas. So the team mapped out the path a burial takes and everyone involved, at every step — a network that included religious figures who lead burial rites, shopkeepers and coffin makers, informal healthcare providers, ambulance drivers, and even nightwatchmen. “These are the people who alert us, and our team is available around the clock to respond, reach the family and seek consent for a sample,” explains Abbas. Mirzaadi is one such woman. She’s spent years as a community health worker in Bhains Colony, logging new families, marriages, births and deaths, long before CHAMPS operated in the area. When her daughter Rafiya was born at Koohi Goth Hospital two years ago, the baby hadn’t cried or urinated since birth. “She was passing discoloured fluid from her mouth,” Mirzaadi recalled. The family was told that the child’s organs were damaged. She was eventually put on a ventilator and died 12 days later. With Mirzaadi not in a state to engage, the project team quickly took consent from her husband Mushtaq, himself a senior research assistant on CHAMPS. The blood culture result following MITS indicated that Rafiya’s likely cause of death was acute gastroenteritis. It wasn’t her kidneys as initially suspected. The culprit was the qehva [green tea] that was given to the newborn. According to Dr Vinod Kumar from The Indus Hospital, common practices such as prelacteal feeding (giving any substance other than breast milk to newborn babies during their first threedays) compromise a baby’s health. “[People say] let’s give honey, or water, or qehva or unpasteurised goat milk,” he tells Eos. Any of them can lead to an infection. MITS has helped families uncover the reason for multiple child deaths. In one case, for example, a virus was detected and treated so the couple’s subsequent children survived. A child infected with Streptococcus pneumoniae, for instance, might also test positive for cytomegalovirus — these opportunistic pathogens strike children who are already sick and more vulnerable. A child placed on a ventilator who then develops ventilator-associated pneumonia, for example, points to a clear, fixable gap: infection control on the equipment itself needs to improve. LOCAL BUGS The pathogens behind neonatal sepsis in Pakistan, according to neonatologist Dr Kumar, look nothing like what doctors encounter in higher-income countries. “We majorly deal with a few of the common bacterial organisms, which include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter, Staphylococcus aureus, and E. coli,” he says, contrasting this with the Group B Streptococcus that dominates in Western neonatal units. Most of these bugs are hospital-acquired — a consequence of overcrowded wards, thin nursing ratios, where “one nurse is looking after four or five babies, or sometimes eight”, making cross-infection almost inevitable. CHAMPS’ initial data supports this. Hospital-acquired and drug-resistant superbug infections, such as Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, occurred overwhelmingly or exclusively in hospitals, showing how drug-resistant bugs thrive in clinical wards The initial data shows a stark contrast between deaths taking place at home and those at a hospital. Measles was the leading cause of death, indicating that these children were not getting their routine immunisation. More troubling was that Streptococcus pneumoniae (six cases) occurred exclusively at home — proof that fatal respiratory infections were killing children before they ever reached a hospital. Among the deaths for which parents consented to MITS, 31 percent were stillbirths, 63 percent involved infants younger than one year of age and six percent occurred among children aged one to five. Although child mortality in these coastal neighbourhoods remains alarmingly high, families now have something they previously lacked: the chance to know exactly why their child died. The writer is a member of staff. She can be contacted at yumnakhan@outlook.com Published in Dawn, EOS, August 2nd, 2026

Asif reacts to Naqvi's call for governance reset, urges him to begin with his own ministry or PCB. Reacting to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s call for an overhaul of the country’s governance structure, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has advised him to initiate the change by implementing the National Action Plan (NAP) and with his own ministry. He also urged him to bring a “revolution” in the Pakistan Cricket Board, which Naqvi heads in addition to the interior ministry. Speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit on Thursday, Naqvi had said the governance system in the country had “collapsed” and argued that the country needed new administrative units, or provinces, to improve service delivery, accountability and access to justice. He had also said new leadership was needed in the country and argued that the youth wanted justice, merit and jobs rather than stipends and laptops. A day later, the military’s spokesperson also urged political parties to consider an administrative reset for improving governance, arg­uing that the country’s security and stability depe­nded on adapting its governance structure to the requirements of modern times and a growing population. Speaking at a news conference, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said governance had long been identified by the military as a prerequisite for nat­ional security. Further recalling the NAP adopted after the 2014 Army Public School attack, he said its 14-point agenda, unanimously endor­sed by political parties, had also rested on effective governance. On Saturday, Asif reacted to Naqvi’s suggestion in an X post, in which he also mentioned the DG ISPR’s remarks. “Mohsin Naqvi’s sahib expressed his views on the dire state of the system. I more or less personally agree with these views,” he said, calling the interior minister a “powerhouse”. Asif added that as a political worker, he too strongly felt the process of the system’s evolution had been “held captive to factional and personal interests for decades, and it needs to be freed”. He said he had a few requests in this regard, adding: “If the system has to be strengthened and a fundamental change has to be brought about, its forum is Parliament, of which Naqvi sahib is a member. Or this matter could be discussed in the cabinet. “This way, these institutions and the system would strengthen, and the change would be brought about through a constitutional process.” Asif went on to point out Naqvi was also a member of the cabinet, further claiming that he rarely attended parliamentary and cabinet sessions. He said: “In my opinion, [treating] these institutions as irrelevant and making such a big statement to a captive audience after inviting the country’s eminent and respected businessmen doesn’t carry the same weight that speaking at the relevant constitutional forums would have earned.” Asif said Naqvi had been on a “very powerful post” of the system for the past three years. “Had he wanted, he could have spoken about a change in the system or made progress on it during this time,” he said, moving to cite the DG ISPR’s remarks during Friday’s press briefing. The defence minister said the military’s spokesperson had referred to the NAP. “The implementation of one of its points, which is the armed forces’ responsibility, is being done by sacrificing lives. The implementation of the remaining 12 points is the interior ministry’s responsibility, but they have not been implemented. “Mohsin Naqvi sahib , begin the change in the system with the implementation of NAP; begin the change in the system with your ministry. Not just the respected business community, the entire nation is with you,” he added. In a subsequent post, Asif further stated: “Naqvi sahib , systems keep evolving all the time and they should. As an example, bring about a revolution in the PCB; cricket fans are not satisfied with PCB’s performance.” He added that in PCB, “power is entirely in your hands. There is neither any prime minister, nor parliament, nor any outdated system as an obstacle”. Naqvi’s call for a reset of the system and creation of more administrative units has sparked a debate in the country, with the PPP referring the question to its top decision-making forum, the Sindh chief minister flatly rejecting it, Lahore’s lawyers terming it unconstitutional and Sindhi nationalist groups demanding the minister’s resignation. In the recent past, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) — also an ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition — has repeatedly demanded that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre along with MQM-P, has strongly opposed the suggested move.

SSGC assures citizens there is no gas leak, says odourisation plant testing led to complaints. The Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) said on Sunday that complaints of a suspected gas leak near Karachi’s Abul Hasan Isphahani Road since the previous night were due to the testing of odourisation plants during the commissioning of a new pipeline. While gas is often thought to have a distinctive smell, it is in fact odourless. Gas suppliers deliberately add odorants to the gas as a safety measure to alert consumers to potentially life-threatening leaks. In a media alert issued on Sunday, the SSGC said that odourants used to give gas its distinctive smell were added in larger quantities for testing purposes. This resulted in a stronger-than-usual smell, prompting reports of a gas leak from various parts of Karachi. “The SSGC administration wishes to make it clear that all system pressures are normal and that no gas leak of any kind has been reported,” the statement said. “The smell is solely due to the relatively larger quantity of odourants added to the gas during the testing of the odourisation plants.” The company requested its customers to remain calm and continue their regular activities. Gas leaks can be life-threatening, causing explosions and fires as well as death by suffocation. In January, three women suffocated to death, while another fainted in a gas leak incident in an apartment in Rawalpindi’s Bahria Town Phase VII.

Security forces kill mastermind of Hangu police checkpost attack: sources. Security forces have killed the mastermind behind the July 30 attack on a police checkpost in Hangu, which claimed the lives of nine police officials, a senior security official told Dawn on Sunday. Security sources said the slain terrorist was identified as Amir Mauviya, and he was killed during an intelligence-based operation in Hangu’s Chapri Naryab. According to the sources, the slain terrorist held an important position among Fitna-al-Khawarij in Kurram, and was wanted in several other terrorism cases. Fitna-al-Khawarij is a term the state uses for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. The sources added that under Operation 11 Garaj, operations against terrorists had been intensified. The attack on the Khazina Banda checkpost had claimed the lives of nine police personnel, including a deputy superintendent of police, and left 28 injured. Police officials said an exchange of fire had broken out after the terrorists attacked the checkpost, and 15 terrorists were killed in retaliatory action. More recently, two police personnel sustained minor injuries in an improvised explosive device explosion targeting a police van near Pir Zakorhi Bridge near the Peshawar-Islamabad motorway toll plaza on Sunday. On July 29, a policeman was martyred and four terrorists were killed during an operation in Swat’s Matta tehsil, police and security sources said. It was merely five days after a terrorist attack on a joint police checkpost in KP’s Tank district martyred 15 people, including 14 security personnel. Among those martyred were 12 soldiers, two policemen and a government official, the military’s media affairs wing said. It added that the attackers attempted to breach the checkpost’s perimeter, but their attempts were “swiftly and decisively foiled” by security forces, who eliminated 12 terrorists. Inter-Service Public Relations (ISPR) said the attackers then rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall and infrastructure at the checkpost was seriously damaged by the impact of the resulting blast. Security personnel and law enforcers have been coming under attack in KP, which continues to face terrorism. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment released on Saturday, Security personnel deaths in terrorism incidents in KP, excluding merged districts, increased from 12 in June to 38 in July and terrorist deaths from 37 to 108, reflecting a rise by 192pc. But civilian deaths fell from 26 to seven, a decline by 73pc. One peace committee member was also killed. Security personnel deaths in merged districts rose from six to 11 and terrorist deaths fell from 72 to 55. Civilian deaths, meanwhile, rose by 86pc, increasing from seven to 13.

Electoral rolls shrink by 589,458 in less than two months as ECP removes 1.48m deceased voters. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s electoral rolls contracted by 589,458 voters between May 7 and July 2, 2026, as the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) removed a large number of deceased voters from the electoral database, more than offsetting fresh registrations during the period, it emerged on Sunday. According to official ECP statistics analysed by Dawn , the total number of registered voters fell from 137,163,857 on May 7 to 136,574,399 on July 2. A senior ECP official said 895,000 new voters were enrolled during the period, but the deletion of around 1.48 million deceased voters resulted in a net decline of 589,458 voters nationwide. The number of male voters dropped from 73,286,821 to 72,835,859, a decrease of 450,962, while female voters declined from 63,877,036 to 63,738,540, down by 138,496. The reduction narrowed the gender gap among registered voters from about 941,000 to 910,000. Overall, 99 of the country’s 144 districts recorded a decline in registered voters, while 45 districts posted a net increase. Punjab Punjab accounted for the overwhelming share of the decline. The province lost 478,909 voters, with the total falling from 77,955,543 to 77,476,634, representing 81.2 per cent of the nationwide reduction. Nine of the 10 districts with the largest declines were in Punjab. According to ECP figures, Faisalabad recorded the largest decrease, with 41,264 voter entries removed, bringing the district’s total down from 56,18,044 to 55,76,780. It was followed by Sheikhupura, with a decline of 31,783 voters, from 22,68,275 to 22,36,492; Gujranwala, with a drop of 30,302 voters, from 29,79,820 to 29,49,518; and Sialkot, which lost 30,129 voters, bringing the number down from 29,84,882 to 29,54,753. The number of voters in Gujrat dropped by 29,553, followed by Sargodha with a decline of 26,675, Multan with 26,420, Kasur with 24,367 and Bahawalpur with 22,259. Likewise, Khanewal saw a decline of 19,504 voters, Rahim Yar Khan 18,574, Lahore 16,633, Narowal 15,914, Toba Tek Singh 15,395, Rawalpindi 13,577, Mandi Bahauddin 13,480 and Attock 11,180. The number of voters in Nankana Sahib and Muzaffargarh declined by over 10,000 each. Another nine districts saw a decrease of over 5,000 each. These included Okara, which saw a decline of 9,784 voters; Khushab, 8,226; Chakwal, 7,377; Dera Ghazi Khan, 6,755; Wazirabad, 6,723; Rajanpur, 6,621; Kot Addu, 6,358; Lodhran, 6,348; and Chiniot, 5,396. Sindh Sindh recorded the second-largest provincial decline, losing 97,216 voters, with the total dropping from 28,772,963 to 28,675,747. Karachi South recorded the largest decline in the province, with 20,243 fewer voters, making it the only non-Punjab district among the top 10 districts with the biggest declines. The number of voters in the district fell from 13,30,682 to 13,10,439. It was followed by Karachi East, where the removal of 16,873 voters brought the total down from 18,15,780 to 17,98,907. Keamari lost 9,983 voters, Karachi West 8,394, Hyderabad 7,573, Khairpur 7,228 and Sanghar 6,240. KP Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) recorded a comparatively small net decline of 9,046 voters, with the provincial total falling from 23,415,995 to 23,406,949. However, it was the only province where more districts recorded gains than losses. In overall terms, the province lost 9,049 voters, accounting for 1.53 per cent of the total decline. While the number of male voters slipped by 16,884, the number of female voters increased by 7,838. Haripur lost 4,978 votes, followed by Abbottabad with 4,182, Charsadda with 3,946, Kohat with 3,352, Nowshera with 3,313, Lower Dir with 3,153 and DI Khan with 2,895. Other districts to have lost over 2,000 votes included Mardan, Hangu and Bannu. Balochistan In Balochistan, the number of voters declined by 2,226, accounting for a 0.38pc decrease. The total fell from 57,65,008 to 57,62,782, reducing the number of male voters by 6,518 while increasing the number of female voters by 4,292. Loralai and Sibi saw declines of 1,048 and 1,025, respectively. Most districts recorded marginal changes, restricted to two or three digits. Islamabad Capital Territory saw a small decline of 2,061 voters, from 12,54,348 to 12,52,287. Those removed from the electoral rolls comprised 1,118 men and 940 women. Despite the overall decline, 45 districts recorded an increase in registered voters between May 7 and July 2. KP led the gains, with 20 of its 36 districts adding voters. Of Balochistan’s 36 districts, 13 saw an increase, while nine of Sindh’s 30 districts recorded a rise in voter numbers. In Punjab, only three of the province’s 41 districts witnessed an increase in the voter count. In KP, the biggest increase was recorded in Peshawar, which added 4,835 voters, taking the total from 22,46,457 to 22,51,292. Other major gains in the province included Bajaur with 3,797, Lower Dir with 3,153, Buner with 1,738 and Mansehra with 1,603. Other districts with increases of over 1,000 included Malakand, Khyber and South Waziristan (Lower). In Balochistan, Quetta remained ahead with an increase of 4,052 voters, followed by Pishin, which saw an addition of 2,523 voters. In 11 other districts, the increase ranged between 65 and 573. Sindh also saw growth in nine districts. Karachi Central recorded the highest increase in the province, with 4,428 new voters, rising from 22,60,158 to 22,64,586. Jacobabad gained 3,928 voters, Ghotki 2,479, Naushahro Feroze 2,103 and Korangi 1,024. Other districts with nominal growth included Larkana, Malir, Tharparkar and Thatta. In Punjab, only three districts saw gains, which were offset by much larger deletions elsewhere. The largest increase was recorded in Bahawalnagar, where the number of voters surged by 16,094, from 20,12,083 in May to 20,28,177 in July, followed by Sahiwal with 4,755 and Vehari with 1,089.

At least 72 died in Spain's Ceuta migrant rush. At least 72 people died during the mass influx in recent days of migrants into Spain’s Ceuta enclave, when tens of thousands of people mostly swam around the border post from Morocco, local officials said on Sunday. Most of the estimated 60,000 people who rushed into Spain’s north African territory have returned to Morocco since the territory’s largest mass migrant crossing. “The latest figure that we have is 72,” the government’s delegate to Ceuta, Miguel Angel Perez Triano, told reporters, when asked about the number of fatalities. The previous toll was 67 deaths. Spanish police and troops patrolled the streets of Ceuta on Sunday as the enclave largely returned to normal after the sudden mass influx of migrants from Morocco that had occurred between Wednesday and Friday. Only small groups of migrants were still walking around after most who crossed the small border barrier returned voluntarily to Morocco in 48 hours. AFP on Saturday saw migrant minors milling around in a disused industrial park in Ceuta. Others were seen dozing on the pavements outside. “All the children here want to go to (mainland) Spain,” said one of the few adults at the site, Moroccan man Aziz Dabch, 41. The largest migrant rush into the enclave has caused an international crisis for Spain, with European partners criticising Madrid for its immigration policies. Outside a housing project near Ceuta port, Spanish soldiers detained a group of nine tired-looking migrants who were sitting on the pavement, guarded by troops with an armoured car, an AFP reporter said. Small inflatable boats from a rescue unit scoured the waters around the border barrier that extends into the Mediterranean Sea, where a new 500-metre (1,640-feet) floating boom reinforced security. Civil Guard were also taking migrants off a bus to escort them back to the border post to return to Morocco. The border crossing was calm, with groups of workers picking up trash, clothes and rubbish left behind during the mass crossing. Rumours Spain has blamed criminal gangs for spreading rumours that a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on immigration would allow migrants easier passage. Some analysts suggested Morocco could allow migrants to cross the border to put diplomatic pressure on Spain, which has recently improved ties with Rabat’s arch-enemy neighbouring Algeria. In 2021, around 10,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, taking advantage of Morocco easing border controls as a way to pressure Spain. Moroccan officials have so far not offered any statement on the crisis. But some of those who crossed the border said they had heard the border was open — a rumour quickly amplified on social media. The EU said it would hold a video call on Tuesday after 22 bloc members issued a joint open letter calling for an urgent meeting to agree a speedy coordinated response, and to prevent further uncontrolled crossings. Italy on Saturday implemented a one-month suspension of its Schengen agreement with Spain allowing for visa-free movement between borders. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, in a letter to EU leaders, blasted the “selfish” reaction by some EU countries. Pope Leo XIV on Sunday spoke to the situation in Ceuta in his daily prayers on Sunday, saying he was following it “with concern” and hoping for a solution of “peace, stability and justice”.

According to the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD), the Met Office in Latifabad recorded 42mm of rain until 5pm, while the City Office recorded 40mm. Power outages were also reported in Hyderabad. The Hyderabad Electric Supply Company (Hesco) spokesperson claimed that electricity supply remained suspended on 285 of the company’s 722 11kV feeders. In Hyderabad city, which has 166 feeders, 66 feeders were unable to provide electricity, he confirmed. A view of railway station main road submerged with rain water after rainfall on Sunday, — Photo by Umair Ali All major arteries and roads in the city were inundated due to rainfall. Meanwhile, water supply was severely affected as the facilities of the Hyderabad Water and Sewerage Corporation (HWSC) remained without electricity. In the absence of electricity and with roads inundated, business activities were also affected. Trade activities in the City Cloth Market, Tower Market, Anaj Mandi and Latifabad Units 5, 10, 11 and 12 were disrupted as roads remained submerged. A view of Hyder Chowk during rain on Sunday,. — Photo by Umair Ali Elsewhere in Sindh, Mithi district recorded the highest rainfall, at 126mm, until 8am on Sunday, according to the PMD. Bodies of Nepalese climber Nirmal Purja, 3 other mountaineers recovered on Broad Peak: Alpine Club. GILGIT: The bodies of celebrated Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and three other mountaineers accompanying him on a summit of the Broad Peak mountain in Gilgit-Baltistan were recovered on Sunday — three days after all 10 members of the team were reported missing after an avalanche. On Saturday, his expedition organising company Elite Exped announced that all members of the team, which also included Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, had died. The bodies of three climbers were recovered by then, as well as the remains believed to be of a climber from the United States, Naila Kiani of the ACP told Dawn on Sunday. Meanwhile, the ACP announced in a statement that Purja’s body had been found. “The Alpine Club of Pakistan shares this update with profound sorrow. The ground rescue team has reached Nirmal Purja ‘Nims Dai’ at approximately 5,700m on Broad Peak, where three additional bodies have also been sighted, though their identities remain unconfirmed. The ground team will bring the bodies down to the Japanese camp. “Recovery efforts continue under extremely difficult terrain conditions,” the statement said. View this post on Instagram In a subsequent post, the organisation said three other bodies, identified as China’s Wang Zhong and Nepal’s Nima Sherpa and Kili Pemba Sherpa, had also been recovered. The “four identified climbers are currently being brought down to Camp 1 (C1) and downwards by the ground rescue team,” the post said. View this post on Instagram It said ACP continued to monitor the ongoing recovery operation on Broad Peak, and rescuers had also “confirmed the presence of one additional body at a significantly higher elevation”. However, “due to the extremely hazardous terrain and prevailing conditions, it is unlikely that a recovery attempt will be made at this stage,” it added. Prior to the announcements, ACP General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that the ground rescue team was heading towards the advanced base camp on the mountain to carry out the operation. He said that the mountain’s terrain, risk of avalanches and steep slopes were posing challenges in the way of rescue efforts, adding that helicopters could not be employed due to weather conditions. Later, the ACP said in a statement that an eight-member ground team, comprising climbers from Pakistan and Nepal, reached Camp 1 (C1) before 9am. “They will conduct a search and recovery mission on the slopes of Broad Peak under extremely difficult conditions,” the statement added. View this post on Instagram Purja’s expedition team included 10 members, including him. Six of them were Nepalese while there was one each from Pakistan, Oman, the US and China. The bodies of two climbers, Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy and Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung, were recovered on Friday, as well as the remains believed to be of American climber Sarah Mallory Geis. On Saturday, the body of Nepal’s Gyalu Sherpa was also recovered, ACP President Irfan Arshad told Dawn . Kiani told Dawn that on Saturday, five other bodies were also spotted on Broad Peak through aerial reconnaissance. Rising 8,051 metres, Broad Peak is the world’s 12th-highest mountain and a technically difficult climb. Seven years before setting out to summit it, Purja had climbed Annapurna, the 10th-highest mountain in the world, in 2019. He then began taking on other 8,000-metre peaks. He set a record for the fastest ascent of the world’s 14 highest mountains, completing the feat in six months in 2019. He became widely known internationally after the Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, ‘14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible’, was released two years later. The 43-year-old climber also served in the British military with the Gurkhas and ​later in special forces. Elite climbers said Purja was a “charismatic, colourful” character. “If we talk about his ​legacy, it’s hard not to focus on how he was at the forefront of shaking up the high altitude guiding,” British climber Kenton Cool, who has climbed Everest 20 ​times, the most by a non-Sherpa, told Reuters on Saturday. In its announcement of the rescue team reaching Purja’s body, the ACP remembered him as a “man who made the impossible possible”. “He carried the Nepali flag to the highest points on Earth with pride, and his achievements brought new recognition to Nepal’s climbing community […] But his impact reached far beyond any one nation, more than the records themselves, he gave people everywhere a reason to believe that the impossible was simply something no one had dared attempt hard enough yet, inspiring dreamers and climbers across the globe to chase what once seemed unreachable.” The statement said, “His loss on the very mountains he so loved is a devastating blow to the global mountaineering family. But his legacy of pushing limits, of proving that the impossible is only impossible until someone dares to do it, will endure in every climber, everywhere, who follows the trail he blazed. “Our deepest condolences go out to his family, loved ones, and the entire climbing community during this immensely difficult time. Rest well, Nims Dai.” Additional input from Reuters

At least 14 people, including police officials, martyred in suicide attack on Kabal police station in Swat: police. At least 14 people, including police officials, were martyred and at least 18 others injured in a suicide attack on Swat’s Kabal police station on Sunday, police and rescue officials said. Swat police spokesperson Nasir Iqbal Karimi, while speaking to Dawn , confirmed the death toll. Malakand Division Deputy Inspector General of Police Fida Hussain told AFP that police officers were among those martyred. He added that another body, suspected to be that of the bomber, had been brought to the hospital. According to the Swat District Police Officer (DPO) Umar Khan, the suicide bomber detonated explosives after police personnel attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station. The DPO said that the police remained on high alert. “Security forces have cordoned off the area, and an investigation is underway to collect further evidence,“ he added. The explosion occurred near the gate of Kabal police station while hundreds of people were participating in a public demonstration at nearby Kabal Chowk against the recent wave of terrorism in Swat Valley. Police officials inspect the site following a suicide bombing during a protest in Swat district on August 2. — AFP The bodies of nine victims were shifted to Central Hospital Saidu Sharif, while the bodies of five others were moved to Kabal Hospital, where doctors confirmed their deaths, said Rescue 1122 Spokesperson Bilal Ahmed Faizi. The spokesperson added that two of the injured are reported to be in critical condition. The powerful blast caused multiple casualties, prompting an immediate emergency response from police, rescue teams and local authorities. Security personnel also sealed off the area and launched a search operation. The protest had drawn a large crowd from across the district and the attack occurred as the final speaker was addressing the crowd, triggering panic among participants. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. Addressing the gathering before the blast, the speakers condemned the resurgence of terrorism in Swat and demanded that the government ensure lasting peace. They said their movement had a single agenda: the restoration of peace and the elimination of terrorism from the region. The speakers stressed that maintaining law and order and eradicating terrorism were the state’s responsibility, warning that continued insecurity could trigger widespread public unrest, citing recent protest movements in other countries as examples of growing public frustration. The speakers also criticised the authorities for what they described as action against peaceful citizens while terrorists continued to operate in the mountainous areas of Swat. They alleged that terrorists had openly circulated videos on social media and questioned why stronger action had not been taken against them. “Our children deserve education, and our families deserve to live in peace,” one speaker told the gathering. “We have witnessed years of bloodshed. Our mothers, sisters, and daughters have suffered immensely, and we do not want another generation of widows and orphans.” Condemnations pour in President Asif Ali Zardari expressed sorrow over the loss of life and called for a comprehensive investigation into the incident, according to a statement issued by his office on X. President Zardari directed the relevant authorities to provide the best possible medical facilities to those injured. “Terrorists will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to undermine peace, national unity and the writ of the state,” he was quoted as saying. He added that the sacrifices of the KP police were “a source of pride for the entire nation”. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also condemned the blast. “Terrorists cannot demoralise the nation with cowardly attacks,” Kundi was quoted as saying, as per a statement. KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, condemning the incident, sought a report from the KP Inspector General of Police (IGP) and offered condolences to the families of the deceased. “The elements hostile to peace will never be allowed to succeed in their nefarious intentions,” the chief minister was quoted as saying. Earlier in the day, an IED blast near the Peshawar-Islamabad motorway toll plaza injured two policemen in the provincial capital Peshawar. On July 30, a terrorist attack on a police checkpost in Hangu martyred nine policemen. KP has seen an uptick in terrorist activity. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’s monthly security assessment, KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 154 terrorism related deaths in July, compared with 75 in June, representing an increase of 105 per cent.

Inconsistencies in Rs332bn grid revenue flagged. ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Autho­rity member (tariff and finance) has questioned regulatory and accounting inconsistencies of the national grid’s recently-cleared revenue requirement of Rs332 billion, citing what she described as the ‘mirror image’ of receivables and non-transferred assets. Nepra member Amina Ahmed pointed out the financial inconsistencies in a detailed dissenting note on a recent 2-1 majority ruling of the regulator, approving a three-year combined revenue requirement for National Grid Company (NGC) at Rs332bn for FY2022-23, FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 for incorporation into consumer-end tariffs through use-of-system charges (UoSC) The NGC (formerly National Transmission & Despatch Company or NTDC) had sought a total of Rs478bn revenue requirement for three years under the multi-year tariff regime. This included Rs112bn for FY23, followed by 45pc rise to Rs163bn for FY24 and another 25pc rise to Rs203bn for FY25. In a majority decision issued a few days ago, Nepra allowed a total of Rs332bn revenue for three years. This included Rs81.5bn for FY23, with a 17pc increase to Rs95.6bn for FY24 and then 62pc increase to Rs155bn for FY25. As a consequence, Nepra approved UoSC at Rs382 per kiloWatt a month for FY23, Rs455 per kW for FY24 and Rs710 per kW a month for FY25. Nepra member says CPPA liability can’t be treated as loan without matching receivable However, Ms Ahmed challenged the treatment of over Rs19bn, recorded as payable to Central Power Purchasing Agency (CPPA) under the head of current liabilities in NGC’s financial statements for 2023-24. She said the majority decision treated the amount as a loan, subtracted from the NGC’s assets to work out its equity amount. “The diminution in the equity amount has consequently resulted in a proportionate reduction in the permissible return allowed” to the NGC, she wrote. Under the business transfer agreement (BTA) of June 2015, NGC transferred the assets and liabilities pertaining to the Market Operations Undertaking to CPPA. As the carrying value of liabilities so transferred exceeded the carrying value of assets transferred, a net payable arose, representing the shortfall between the two, she said, adding the BTA has since been extended on multiple occasions and amounted to over Rs19bn as of June 30, 2024. Correspondingly, an offsetting balance was recognised under the current assets with details given in the Advances and Other Receivables, reflecting an amount recoverable by NGC from certain power sector entities. “A certain portion of these receivables represents the mirror image of the asset not transferred to CPPA,” she said, adding that had this receivable also been transferred to CPPA as part of the same BTA transaction, no such liability would have remained on NGC’s books. Separately, as per Nepra mechanism, the equity amount was to be computed by aggregating fixed assets and current assets, and then deducting the non-current and current liabilities. “The methodology does not rely upon the actual current assets and current liabilities as reported in the financial statements; instead, they are derived by applying certain prescribed formulae,” she said, arguing that while Nepra guidelines provided formula for computing current assets, the current liabilities, as per the practice, were instead taken as a fixed proportion, i.e. 2/3 of the current assets so arrived at. As a consequence, she argued that the amount due to CPPA bore no nexus whatsoever with the financing of NGC’s long-term assets. “Accordingly, this amount cannot be equated with loans (long-term) employed for financing the assets... They represent two sides of the same net position; recognising one without the other produces a distorted equity amount,” the member said. “Either both should be netted off against each other, or both excluded, selectively recognising only the liability, while ignoring its corresponding asset, is not correct,” she added. Naqvi’s call for new provinces faces fresh pushback. ISLAMABAD: Key lea­ders of coalition partners, reacting to Interior Min­ister Mohsin Naqvi’s proposal to overhaul the country’s governance stru­cture and create new provinces , urged him to first implement the National Action Plan (NAP), arguing that Pakistan’s governance fail­ures stem from constitutional violations rather than the existing federating units. Defence Minister Kha­waja Asif responded to Mr Naqvi’s remarks in a post on X, in which he also referred to the DG ISPR’s comments . “Mohsin Naqvi sahib expr­essed his views on the dire state of the system. I more or less personally agree with these views,” Mr Asif wrote, describing the interior minister as a “powerhouse”. He added that, as a political worker, he believed the country’s political evolution had been “held captive to factional and personal interests for decades” and needed to be freed. The federal minister advised Mr Naqvi to begin the overhaul process by implementing NAP through his own ministry. He also urged Mr Naqvi to bring about a “revolution” in the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), which he heads in addition to serving as interior minister. Last week, Mr Naqvi had said the country’s governance system had “collapsed” and argued that Pakistan needed new administrative units, or provinces, to improve service delivery, accountability and access to justice. He also called for new leadership, saying the country’s youth wanted justice, merit and jobs rather than stipends and laptops. A day later, the military’s spokesperson also called on political parties to consider an administrative reset to improve governance, arguing that the country’s security and stability depended on adapting its governance structure to the demands of modern times and a growing population. Mr Asif said that if the system was to be str­engthened and meaningful reforms introduced, the appropriate forum was parliament, of which Mr Naqvi is a member, or the federal cabinet. “This way, these institutions and the system would be strengthened, and change would come through a constitutional process,” he said. The defence minister also pointed out that Mr Naqvi was a cabinet member but claimed he rar­ely attended parliamentary or cabinet sessions. “In my opinion, treating these institutions as irrelevant and making such a major statement before a captive audience after inviting the country’s eminent and respected businessmen does not carry the same weight that it would have had if made at the relevant constitutional forums,” he said. Mr Asif further noted that Mr Naqvi had held a “very powerful position” in the system for the past three years. “Had he wanted, he could have spoken about changing the system or made progress on it during this time,” he said. In a subsequent post on X, Mr Asif also urged Mr Naqvi to reform the Pakistan Cricket Board. “Naqvi sahib, systems evolve continuously and they should. As an example, bring about a revolution in the PCB. Cricket fans are not satisfied with its performance,” he wrote. He added that in the PCB, “all authority rests with you. There is neither a prime minister, nor parliament, nor any outdated system standing in your way.” Rabbani opposes new provinces Meanwhile, former Senate chairman Mian Raza Rabbani has strongly opposed the proposal to create new provinces, arguing that Pakistan’s governance failures stem from violations of the Constitution rather than the existing federating units. In a detailed statement, he cautioned that redrawing administrative boundaries would not resolve the country’s deep-rooted systemic issues. Instead, he said, the real causes of the governance crisis are the erosion of provincial autonomy and the weakening of democratic institutions. According to the veteran lawmaker, several factors have contributed to the current situation. These include the repeated derailment of the democratic process, the ceding of political space to the civil-military bureaucracy, the weakening of the federation through the centralisation of powers in Islamabad, allowing dictators to amend the Constitution at will, experimenting with more than 10 models of governance since 1947, policy decisions being taken outside parliament, rendering it redundant, the failure to hold free, fair elections as envisaged, governance being carried out in blatant violation of the Constitution, disregard for the doctrine of the trichotomy of powers, the prevalence of rule by law instead of the rule of law, and the denial of provincial autonomy. “This is just the tip of the iceberg,” Mr Rabbani said. The veteran politician also proposed several measures to address the country’s governance challenges. These include strict adherence to the supremacy of the Constitution, 1973; upholding the rule of law; ensuring full compliance with the provincial autonomy guaranteed under the Constitution, 1973; strict observance of the constitutional principle of the trichotomy of powers; and devolving political, administrative, and financial authority to elected local governments as envisaged under Article 140-A of the Constitution, 1973.
