Balochistan govt orders inquiry into Sorange coal mine disaster. • Balochistan Chief Minister’s Inspection Team tasked with determining causes, fixing responsibility for negligence • Four mines sealed as separate departmental inquiry launched QUETTA: The Balochistan government has ordered a high-level inquiry into the deadly coal mine disaster in Sorange that claimed the lives of 34 miners, assigning the investigation to the Chief Minister’s Inspection Team (CMIT) to determine the causes of the tragedy and identify those responsible. On the directives of Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti, the CMIT, headed by its chairman Bashir Ahmed Bangulzai, will conduct an on-site investigation into the July 30 accident. The inquiry has been tasked with establishing the actual cause of the incident, reviewing the performance of the relevant authorities, fixing responsibility for any negligence, and proposing measures to prevent similar accidents in the future. According to an official notification issued on Sunday, the CMIT has been directed to submit its findings and recommendations to the chief minister within two weeks. Mines sealed Separately, the mines and minerals department has also initiated a departmental inquiry into the incident. Authorities have sealed four coal mines, including the two directly affected by the accident, as part of the ongoing investigation. The Sorange mine disaster, one of the deadliest mining accidents in Balochistan in recent years, claimed the lives of 34 miners after they were trapped 3,000 to 4,000 feet deep inside the coal mine. Balochistan Chief Inspector of Mines Muhammad Atif said all 34 coal miners hailed from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Shangla district. Abid Yaar, president of the Shangla Coal Mine Workers Association, said Mian Kalay in Shangla’s Pirabad town, from where 23 of the miners hailed, had become an epicentre of repeated coal mine tragedies. He added that the victims, aged between 17 and 25, belonged to the same families and were cousins or close relatives. According to Mr Yaar, several of the deceased were orphans whose fathers had also lost their lives in previous coal mine accidents. The tragedy has renewed concerns over mine safety standards, regulatory oversight and enforcement of safety protocols in the province’s coal mining sector. Officials said the findings of the investigations would help determine accountability and guide future reforms aimed at improving worker safety and preventing similar tragedies. Deadly mine explosions are common in Balochistan, with stakeholders often pointing out the abse­nce of essential safety protocols. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

Labour in a changing world. “The times, they are a-changin,” is a 1964 iconic song by legendary Bob Dylan. Times have even changed and evolved in the world of work, even in the Pakistani industrial relations ecosystem. Gone are the days when ego-centric labour leaders wielded influence on members, energising them with demagoguery and rabble-rousing. Gone are the days when they would exert their self-generated importance to browbeat and intimidate employers. Within a few years, they faded away in the sunset. They rarely developed their successors. Narcissism prevailed over pragmatism. A new cadre of labour leaders gradually came to the fore, but by that time the worker movement had lost steam, and the number of labour unions across the country had substantially declined; today, only about one per cent of enterprises have registered unions. This new cadre faced, and is still facing, a difficult task in motivating workers to form unions and display brotherhood. They are reasonably successful in stimulating unions in the public sector but have to move boulders, cross turbulent seas, and remove bottlenecks to achieve entry into targeted individual enterprises. The Pakistan United Workers Federation was formed through the merger of ten moderate labour federations. PUWF is the largest and represents over one million workers in 637 unions. The next large federations are the National Labour Federation and the Pakistan Central Mines Workers Federation. However, most workers’ federations lack the critical mass to build a movement to register unions and have their voices heard in the corridors of power. Although major political parties do have their wings or bureaus, the latter seldom have a formidable say in the parties’ policies. There are labour leaders who are still in a time warp. Their speeches revolve around three or four issues that are ignored by employers and, to some extent, by the government. Their favourite is the issuance of appointment letters for workers because, in their opinion, an appointment letter guarantees job security, even though any worker who is underperforming, displays signs of hostility, or is a chronic absentee will soon be chucked out. Even if that worker knocks at the portals of the courts and even if reinstated, that worker will undoubtedly face resistance from management. Another beef against employers, and this is a genuine complaint, is that the prescribed minimum wage is not given to most of the workers. The minimum wage for unskilled workers provides an essential floor of protection, helps prevent exploitation, and supports the welfare of vulnerable workers. The difficulty for employers arises when the Minimum Wage Board sets wages for semi-skilled and skilled workers, since it may not be in the broader interest of industry and labour market dynamics. Skills, productivity, experience, specialisation, market demand, and sectoral requirements generally determine wages of semi-skilled and skilled workers. Such wages are more appropriately regulated through market mechanisms, collective bargaining, and enterprise-level arrangements. In the majority of countries, a single minimum wage is announced by the government, which ensures that it is paid to every worker. It is standard practice and an accepted norm that the employer determines the wages of skilled employees. A skilled worker will not accept minimum wage unless in dire circumstances. Then there is the mantra of what labour leaders refer to as contract workers. This system is more aptly known as outsourcing of manpower or business functions or third-party employment. It is an employment arrangement in which workers perform services for a principal employer but are formally employed by another entity, such as a contractor, service provider, or outsourcing company. Third-party employment is widely used in both the private and public sectors, particularly for labour-intensive functions or those requiring staffing flexibility. They prefer third-party employment for specific reasons, such as operational flexibility, cost efficiency, specialised expertise, business focus, risk management, and project-based employment. Although there is no bar to outsourcing, this system cannot and should not be used as a means to circumvent existing labour laws. Labour leaders agitate over this issue because such workers cannot join the enterprise union, as they are technically employees of the service provider. On the other extreme, some labour leaders possess a negative attitude and are instrumental in promoting and enriching themselves by disseminating complaints against local enterprises, especially garment and knitwear units, to their foreign associates. These foreign entities, usually radical activists, pump up these complaints by sending them to brands that import from Pakistan and strongly demanding that they cease business with that unit. Although it is much ado about nothing, it impacts the nation’s image as well as exports. The world has changed dramatically over the last few decades, and this transformation is a result of increasing globalisation of business, the growth of multinational corporations, the climate crisis, privatisation, and the rapid pace of technological change. Workers must join hands with employers and agitate for the rationalisation of heavy taxation measures, vociferously condemn and denounce the increase in blatant extortion demands on businesses by extremists and criminals, and influence the government to introduce favourable policies to spur industrialisation. Bob Dylan’s message must be absorbed by labour leaders who are still trapped in a time warp. The lyrics are captivating: “Admit that the waters / Around you have grown / And accept it that soon / If your time to you is worth savin’ / And you better start swimmin’ / Or you’ll sink like a stone / For the times they are a-changin’. The writer is the president of the Employers Federation of Pakistan Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 3rd, 2026

Woman bomber kills 3 near Moscow restaurant. MOSCOW: A homemade bomb carried by a woman killed at least three people and injured 21 near an upscale restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, authorities said, amid unconfirmed speculation on social media that the attack may have been linked to the war in Ukraine. REN TV cited a source on Sunday as saying that two people who had been taken to hospital had later died of their wounds, bringing the death toll to five, though there was no official confirmation. Unverified social media reports suggested that a top Russian military commander had been the intended target but had been unharmed. Living with leopards in the Himalayas. In the afternoon of Feb 22, 67-year-old Bulal Maharjan, a farmer on the outskirts of Kathmandu, was sitting on his porch chopping cauliflower leaves to feed his chickens. Hearing a loud thud as a parked motorcycle toppled, he turned and watched in horror as a leopard leapt away from the fallen vehicle and lunged at him, piercing its sharp canines into his forehead, its claws lacerating his hands. Within seconds, neighbours swarmed in, and the leopard ran into a nearby house. They eventually trapped the animal inside. After nearly two hours of panic that saw two more people injured trying to control the distressed big cat, forest division officials managed to sedate it and bring the situation under control. Maharjan still can’t shake off memories of the attack. “For three days straight, I couldn’t even sleep. Every time I began to doze, the scene of this attack would jolt me up!” he says. “I think we should just get rid of this animal. Period.” Conflicts with people are growing as expanded forest land and climate change push the creatures into human settlements Sentiments like Maharjan’s are common across Nepal, where leopards have been responsible for significant loss of human life and livestock. Research shows that from the years 2000 to 2020, conflicts between humans and four large mammals — elephants, rhinos, tigers and common leopards — claimed 887 human lives and led to the killing of 1,139 animals. Of these, common leopards were the leading cause of human deaths at an average of 19 deaths per year, and the species most frequently killed. To try to bring the conflict under control, Nepal and other countries with human-large predator conflicts are exploring a range of solutions. Nepal has three ecological zones: lowland dominated by Bengal tigers, mountainous regions where snow leopards roam free, and the vast mid-hill ruled by common leopards as the top predator. While protected areas in the lowlands and mountains receive dedicated conservation funding for their charismatic predators, the mid-hills are largely managed as community forests. The celebrated community forest program is a key reason for leopards’ thriving in the mid-hills. In the early 1990s, amid worsening floods and landslides linked to forest degradation, King Birendra handed over management of large swaths of forest to local communities so that they would have stakes in conservation, and benefit from timber and fruit harvests. Today, almost 47 per cent of Nepal is covered by forest patches. About a third of that area belongs to community forests, most of which are run by people living in the mid-hills. “But what the communities didn’t realise was they also restored habitats so that the top carnivores could return,” said Kedar Baral, a wildlife biologist for Nepal’s Bagmati province. In 2020, Baral’s team conducted an analysis of leopard scat collected in the mid-hills that showed that 27pc of the animals’ diet consisted of domestic animals, while the wild ungulates that big cats typically prefer to hunt, like barking deer and wild boars, made up only 10pc. In search of sprouting leaves, barking deer venture from the dense community forests to farmland, and “as the deer enter the farmlands, that’s where the leopard follows,” says Baral, bringing them into contact with domestic livestock. Nepal’s hydropower and construction projects are also expanding into remote forested areas at higher elevations, disturbing habitat and bringing workers as well as a new hunting pressure against top predators, including common leopards, living there. That forces the leopards and their prey to leave their territory, says Madhu Chetri, a wildlife ecologist at the National Trust for Nature Conservation. Climate change might be influencing conflict patterns, too. While he was working as a district forest officer in Nepal’s western mid-hills, Baral and his team were repeatedly called to respond to common leopard attacks on local communities. Over time, he noticed a change in the pattern: Conflict incidents and human or livestock deaths were increasingly reported from higher-elevation settlements. Reporting in 2023, Baral and colleagues investigated whether climate change was driving this shift. Using data from 343 sites across Nepal based on signs of leopard scat, animal tracks and kills, he modeled habitat preferences of leopards, considering factors such as temperature, rainfall and elevation. The results suggest that leopards prefer mid-hill conditions at around 1,000 meters with moderate temperatures and high rainfall. Warming climates are likely expanding the range of suitable habitat uphill, which could allow the leopard population to grow and, as a result, have a higher risk of conflict with humans. Of course, it is a conservation success to be celebrated when numbers of threatened or endangered large carnivores increase — whether they be lynx, wolves, tigers or leopards — but it also presents new challenges, says Philip Nyhus, a conservation biologist at Colby College in Maine. Solutions to the problem have two parts, he adds: first, to keep wildlife separate from people and their livestock to prevent conflict to begin with, and second, to mitigate impacts when conflicts do occur. “A lot of attention has been given to the second piece,” he says. “What would be better is if we could prevent conflict from happening in the first place.” There are international examples to draw from. In the Argentinian Dry Chaco forest, for example, small households in woody areas have faced frequent attacks by pumas on sheep and goats. Sofia Nanni, a conservation biologist at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council of Argentina, worked with locals to come up with the idea of trying spiked leather collars on livestock, an approach that had proved successful in reducing leopard attacks on cows in countries like Iran. “We found a local artisan who made collars for dogs and we asked him if he could make collars,” Nanni says. Tracking collared goats and sheep for two years, her team found that the puma predation in uncollared animal groups was 10 times higher than that in collared groups. Several other strategies are successfully reducing leopard and other top predator conflicts globally. Still, changing attitudes and implementing effective interventions, as well as better compensation, can take years, while frustration among affected communities continues to grow. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

Damage assessment. PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit an all-time low according to the latest Economist/YouGov poll. The survey found 62 per cent of Americans disapprove of the president’s performance while 63pc say the country is headed in the wrong direction. These are Trump’s worst numbers since he returned to the White House last year. The results align with findings of other polls, which show he has fallen out of favour with the majority of Americans. The slide isn’t just about an unpopular war with Iran. Trump’s management of the economy is also driving public discontent. The first 18 months of the mercurial leader’s second term have been defined by disruption at home and abroad. His ‘America First’ unilateralism has meant military strikes on multiple countries and upending of the global trading system. It reflects contempt for international law and other nations’ sovereignty. For a president who promised to end wars, not start them, his record is the opposite. Trump assumed American power could browbeat other countries into compliance at no cost to the US. That was a miscalculation. His overreliance on force also failed to produce the results he wanted. Trump may be extreme in his imperious, unilateralist ways but there is continuity with past US conduct in an important respect. Throughout its history of dealing with other nations, the US has underestimated the power of nationalism and the resistance it would meet in trying to force its will on others. It found that in its interventions in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq, which entangled Washington in unwinnable wars, produced strategic blunders and doomed its military adventures. Today, it is finding that again in the war against Iran. Trump also doesn’t seem to understand that the unipolar world long passed into history. In today’s multipolar world, countries will not so easily bend to Washington’s will. Indeed, the more Trump makes blusterous claims and tweets about how he has the power to get what he wants, the more it exposes his inability to secure his goals. There is no shortage of commentary on Donald Trump’s personality and record. Two of the latest books are worth noting. Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan and Betrayed: America didn’t vote for this by Ira Shapiro and Anne Kim. Both cover the first year plus of Trump’s second presidency and deliver stinging indictments of his performance. Betrayed is written by a broad coalition of distinguished bipartisan experts from among former government officials, lawyers, scholars and journalists. They are members of what is called the Common Sense Coalition. They chronicle the damage Trump has done to his country and to America’s standing in the world. This damage assessment is undertaken across multiple areas — economy, foreign policy, democracy and free speech, judiciary, voting system, education and climate. The book’s main point is that Americans did not vote for what Trump is doing and the disorder he is producing. His abuses of power must be stopped and his team members held accountable if America’s crisis is to end. With his approval ratings having plunged Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes towards the US. Though brief the chapters are pointed. The one on a weaker America is especially sharp. It argues that Trump has fractured the foundations for global stability. His costly and impetuous military adventures without a strategy or respect for international law and his contempt for traditional allies have endangered US security. The authors describe an unchecked president dragging the country into multiple conflicts with scant regard for the fallout. The attack on Iran, they argue, lays bare the hallmarks of his foreign policy decision making — impulsiveness, prioritising force over diplomacy, failure to take rational decisions based on their likely impact and trashing the concerns of allies. They frame his National Security Strategy as a reversal of eight decades of US foreign policy. This has resulted in ‘America Weaker’ and ‘America Alone’ and drained its soft power. Its international stature has diminished. Trump has alienated virtually all allies who had helped the US maintain global peace. The authors also argue Trump has misused and politicised the military and packed it with yes-men afraid of telling him the truth. In the chapter on the rule of law the writers hold Trump guilty of violating limits on presidential power, threatening the integrity of courts and usurping Congressional powers. Core civil liberties have been threatened. He is seen as weaponising government machinery including the Justice Department to punish political opponents and suppress dissent. He has violated court orders and vilified judges while shielding his friends from legal accountability. Regime Change is no less scathing about Trump’s record in office. Its subtitle Inside the imperial presidency of Donald Trump indicates its focus is on the inner workings of the White House. It is a riveting, richly sourced account of the chaos wreaked by a president who has acted with impunity and radically changed the office he occupies. It narrates how efforts have been made to stop Trump but failed. Based on over 1,000 interviews, it takes the readers behind the scenes to offer insights into Trump’s decision-making that has been so consequential and of course harmful for the country. How his team fell in line with his decisions even when they strongly disagreed is exemplified by a telling exchange between Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu during his February visit to Washington when he convinced Trump to attack Iran. The Israeli leader assured Trump that regime change would succeed in Iran and its nuclear capability would be destroyed, before Tehran could seize the Strait of Hormuz. The CIA director rubbished this view while the secretary of state called it “farcical”. But Trump prevailed. Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes toward the US. Friends, allies and adversaries view the erratic swings in American policy with alarm. The latest poll by the Pew Research Centre captures the shift. China is viewed more favourably than the US in most countries surveyed. Given the turbulence of the past 18 months, that result is hardly unexpected. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

A hard state?. THESE days we are repeatedly told that the Pakistani state has been soft on anarchy for far too long. This is the considered and stated position of many state officials as well as of many supporters of those in power. Common people may hold any number of positions that one finds distasteful but the same sentiments being voiced by those in power invite both scrutiny and concern. For the last three years, there has been much chatter about turning Pakistan into a ‘hard state’. No one has given an adequate definition of what this entails, but based on disparate statements and impulses, we can gather this has something to do with protecting the rights of the state and the decision-makers who staff it. These rights are being obtained via a frequently violent trade-off with the rights of the people of Pakistan. The projected consequence of such a trade-off is that protest of all shades becomes a privilege. Demands can only be voiced with due approval through vetted content and NOCs. Speech is to be regulated via defamation, criminalisation laws, and an apparently pliant judiciary till it takes on an acceptable hue, or preferably till it becomes an echo of the state’s. These impulses are neither unique to the Pakistani state nor are they exceptional to this current moment. Trysts with authoritarianism dot the country’s past and arguably lie at the roots of its state structure. British viceregal authority bequeathed an overdeveloped administrative apparatus, which has since then done exceedingly well to reproduce itself and the privileges of those who staff it. When given a chance, politicians of nearly all stripes — centralists, federalists, provincial magnates, or constituency-level bigwigs — have been more than happy to fortify this arrangement for their own and their clients’ benefits. And yet there is a question that should gnaw at anyone who thinks about the trade-off at the table. What is all of this for? If people are being asked to voluntarily or otherwise forfeit their constitutional or social rights, it only makes sense to interrogate what end goal this forfeiture is designed to serve. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Forfeiture of individual liberty is commanded by all states in service of some basic objectives. Usually the foremost of these objectives is territorial sanctity: no state tolerates geographic loss and will usually strip people of their rights, property and lives to prevent it. The Pakistani state is fairly typical in this manner. It deals with separatism/secessionism the way many other post-colonial states do, and with variable degrees of success. The bigger question on that front then is whether its strategy for preventing the rise or growth of this factor is useful at all. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Other states offer different types of answers. The case of China — paradigmatic for the 21st century — has a very simple one. It places limits on various forms of individual rights for the protection and promotion of the CCP’s endeavours. The main endeavour, since the 1970s at least, has been the growth and collective prosperity of the Chinese people via the unleashing of productive forces (labour and capital), both by the state and by private enterprise. The state under one-party rule decides the degree of this unleashing, its objectives, and ultimately the distribution of its fruits. In the previous century, socialist states decided that the true fulfilment of human life lay in getting rid of privatised forms of exploitation. And so a suspension of individual liberty was done in service of collective ownership of resources, commandeered by the state. Social democratic states in Western Europe decided to infringe on the rights of capital owners over their profit in order to redistribute benefits to the working class via taxation. The late-20th-century Asian Tigers took away social rights of the working poor to generate double-digit capitalist growth. There are other, less palatable answers too. The fascists in Germany stripped the rights, property, and lives of one minority group and various ideological dissenters (primarily the communists) in service of its ethnonationalist and expansionist agenda. At present, the ruling party in India targets individual liberties of specific segments, such as Muslims, to fulfil the cultural agenda of its majority base. In all of these examples, the use of state power is for some larger agenda; a larger agenda in the name of the public (or at least an important part of it), built on specific ideational values and postulates. Something being done in service of something bigger, grander, and to varying degrees, collective. So one must pose the question: what objective does this particular, three-year-old vintage of the ‘hard state’ serve in Pakistan? To date there is no coherent answer. We do not know what the killing of protesters — regardless of the agreeability of their demands — in AJK is going to achieve. What goal banning political movements in the peripheries serves. What Form-47ing election outcomes does. What the hollowing out of the opposition, judiciary, media or civil society helps obtain. If the answer is to maintain territorial integrity, then the vast majority of those whose rights stand stripped away carry no geographic ambitions. If the answer is to unleash GDP growth rates of the kind unseen in the last two decades, then one must reluctantly point out that the needle is yet to move up at all. If the answer is to project sovereignty and stature on the world stage at a time of global upheaval, the logical follow-up is a) whose stature and b) sovereignty in whose name? There are no ready grand answers at the end of this line of inquiry because there is likely no grand thought among those steering the ‘hardening’. The actual answers, if one were to hazard a guess, are probably several degrees more modest: the prolonging of duration in office, an improvement in personal quality of life, and the distribution of gifts and sinecures to a small coterie of loyalists at the expense of everyone else. Farewell to arms?. PALESTINIAN resistance group Hamas recently made a major concession by agreeing to give up its weapons. It should be remembered that along with its political activities, the movement has an armed wing dedicated to the liberation of Palestine. The group’s weapons will be surrendered to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian technocratic body formed under US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. In essence, Hamas has thrown the gauntlet to Israel: it is ready to surrender its weapons, but will the Zionist state end its occupation of Gaza? This remains the million-dollar question. Mr Trump was upbeat about the development, saying that Israel was “very happy” about it. However, while there had been no official reaction from Tel Aviv at the time of writing, most Israeli politicians, including some in the cabinet, have decried the move, calling for the destruction of Hamas. It will be interesting to see whether Israel honours its end of the deal and vacates occupied Palestinian territory in Gaza. Going by past precedent, the Israelis are not known for keeping their word. Also, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an election in October , and there is widespread anti-Palestinian sentiment amongst the electorate. But the Israeli leader may not want to annoy the American president by appearing to sabotage Mr Trump’s Gaza peace plan. Lest we forget, Israel has murdered over 73,000 Palestinians — more than 21,000 of them children — since the Oct 7, 2023 attacks, and while its killing spree has lessened in intensity, it has not stopped completely since the ceasefire came into effect last year. Moreover, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains appalling. It should be kept in mind that Hamas and other Palestinian groups have continued their armed struggle against Israel because the Zionist state has closed all avenues of peacefully resolving the Palestine question. Almost the entire Israeli political class is opposed to a Palestinian state, illegal settlements continue to proliferate, and Gaza — which even before the 2023 attacks was virtually under siege — lies in ruins. Meanwhile, Israeli provocations against Al Aqsa have not stopped. If this situation is to change, there must be a clear pathway for a Palestinian state, an end to Israeli brutalities against the Arab population, and complete withdrawal from all occupied territories. Knowing the current political climate in Israel, this is asking for the moon. However, Mr Trump, who sees himself as a ‘peacemaker’, and his BoP must press Israel to at least start the process by withdrawing from Gaza, and allowing unimpeded humanitarian assistance into the Strip. If Tel Aviv does not leave Gaza, it will show the world that it is not serious about peace, and is committed to the occupation of Palestine and to the extermination of the Palestinian people. Criminal record verification of Lahore's commercial drivers in the offing. LAHORE: The city traffic police have initiated verification of the criminal record of 348,000 commercial vehicle drivers following reports that they were involved in 48 percent of the total fatal road crashes. The decision was taken during a high-level meeting, where official data pertaining to repeated crashes and unsafe driving history of commercial and public service vehicles was presented. Chaired by Chief Traffic Officer (CTO) Syed Abdul Raheem Shirazi, the meeting reviewed the growing trend of commercial vehicle-related crashes and formulated a strategy to address the underlying causes. SP Headquarters Fakhar Bashir Raja had been assigned a special mandate to conduct an in-depth analysis of crash patterns and recommend evidence-based interventions to prevent future fatalities. A traffic police spokesperson said that the meeting was informed that Lahore had approximately 8.2 million registered vehicles, including 348,000 commercial vehicles, representing nearly five percent of the city’s total registered vehicle fleet. Despite their relatively small share, he said, commercial vehicles were involved in 48 percent of fatal road crashes, underscoring the need for immediate regulatory and enforcement measures. Traffic police data shows commercial drivers involved in 48pc of all fatal road crashes The meeting passed directions to the relevant police officers for the verification of the criminal background, driving history, licence status, and overall eligibility of every commercial and public service vehicle driver. “Drivers with criminal records, a history of repeated traffic crashes, habitual traffic violations, or conduct posing a threat to public safety will not be granted permits or licences to operate commercial vehicles,” said CTO Sherazi. He said that transport unions and commercial vehicle owners had been instructed to ensure that no driver was employed or entrusted with a vehicle without proper background verification, including a valid character certificate and complete record clearance. The move would help bring down serious and fatal traffic crashes across the provincial capital, the CTO said and warned that vehicle owners and transport operators who knowingly employ or facilitate high-risk drivers would also be held accountable under the law. “Accountability will extend beyond negligent drivers to those who enable them. Owners who disregard safety standards by allowing unfit drivers to operate commercial vehicles will face strict legal action,” he said. The meeting also resolved to undertake verification of driving licences of all commercial and public service vehicle drivers and granted approval for strict enforcement action against individuals found operating vehicles with fake, forged, expired, suspended, or otherwise invalid driving licences. Justin Greaves steadies West Indies in second Test against Pakistan. Justin Greaves made an unbeaten 64 to steer West Indies to 239-5 at stumps on a rain-shortened opening day of the second and final Test against Pakistan in Trinidad on Sunday. After a match-winning display with the ball in the first Test last week, Greaves displayed what has now become his trademark ease and composure at the crease in a battling knock at Queen’s Park Oval. His only error of judgement came just after reaching the half-century mark when captain Babar Azam put down a straightforward chance at leg-slip off spinner Sajid Khan. Greaves at that time was almost hobbling after a left leg injury sustained while completing a sharp run that necessitated lengthy treatment on the field. His sixth-wicket partnership with Roston Chase (36 not out) was worth 66 runs at the close of play and Greaves will be hoping for a return to his usual athletic mobility when he resumes the innings with his captain on the second morning. He had come to the crease in mid-afternoon at 91 for three as Kavem Hodge became Khan’s first wicket. When Amir Jangoo fell to a leg-side catch to give debutant pacer Ubaid Shah his first Test wicket with the first ball of a new spell, Pakistan sensed the chance to break the back of the West Indies resistance. However Greaves and Shai Hope provided a measure of stability in a 53-run stand until seamer Mohammad Ali, the most impressive of the bowlers on the day, bowled Hope off the inside-edge for 29 to leave the innings in the balance at 173 for five. Pakistan omit Abbas Earlier, Pakistan’s bewildering decision-making — on and off the field of play — highlighted a rain-affected morning session. Mohammad Abbas, the tourists’ best bowler by some distance from the 90-run defeat in the first Test, was dropped despite a match haul of eight for 85, including five for 22 in the second innings. A second Pakistani debutant, Awais Zafar, got his chance due to the finger injury sustained by former captain Shan Masood while compiling a determined century in the first Test. Pakistan’s think-tank seemed convinced of the wisdom of playing an additional slow bowler on a surface devoid of grass, drafting in Khan as an off-spinning option alongside left-arm orthodox bowler Ali Usman, who went wicketless on debut in the first Test. Khan’s first notable act in the match was to take the catch at long-leg which sent Tagenarine Chanderpaul to the pavilion for 15 as he failed to control a hook shot off Mohammad Ali after a brisk opening stand of 49 with Brandon King. “We needed those partnerships at the end of the day and it was good to see those guys (Greaves, Hope and Chase) making those contributions,” said King in summing up the day’s effort. “It would be nice if we get more of the same from them tomorrow and Justin and Roston can go on to get hundreds.” As easily as the runs flowed, especially off King’s bat, in the early exchanges after Chase opted to bat first, both could have been dismissed earlier with more attacking tactics as they each benefited from edges at catchable height through the vacant third slip position. Mohammad Ali was even pleading with Babar for additional support in the slip cordon following the third of those fortunate escapes. King’s luck ran out though following the 90-minute rain break as Usman snared him for his first Test wicket, leg-before for 46.

Trump says new Iran talks set to start today after calling off massive attack. US President Donald Trump said that new negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the country to pursue a deal to end the war entering its sixth month. Trump told reporters on Sunday that the talks would cover the Strait of Hormuz — a route for global energy supplies that has become a key sticking point in the conflict —and ultimately, the denuclearisation of Iran. For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait, where a tanker reported an explosion nearby on Sunday, underscoring the continued volatility of the strategic waterway. Oil prices fell on Monday at the opening of Asian trade after Trump announced the new negotiations, with West Texas Intermediate dropping 4.7 per cent to $80.72 per barrel. Washington and Tehran have been at war since February 28, when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, though months of on-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm. Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran “very hard” and was reportedly considering renewed attacks including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert. Trump pulled back from that threat on Saturday, saying the “parameters” of a deal were there. “Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants in the talks. The US president said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes, which he claimed would have been “the biggest attack since World War II”. Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike. A previous ceasefire deal that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fell through, and Iran has since tightened its control over the waterway. The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran’s nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature. ‘Exchange of views’ Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament’s national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June. That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz. “They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views,” Ghashghavi said. Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, “We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed.” Iran deal with Oman? Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects. That dispute sparked the return to strikes last month, as Tehran refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast. On Sunday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides—neither the northern route nor the southern route — but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said. He insisted though that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait. Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply. On Sunday, a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion near the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, adding that the vessel and crew were all safe.

Oil tumbles as Trump cancels attack on Iran to reach deal aimed at reopening Hormuz. Oil prices tumbled more than $4 a barrel on Monday after US President Donald Trump held off on a fresh attack on Iran, seeking to reach a quick deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures slid $4.49, or 5.11 per cent, to $83.44 by 0408 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $79.77 a barrel, down $4.90, or 5.79pc. Both contracts jumped more than 20pc last month after fighting between the US and Iran resumed and as attacks on several tankers around Oman heightened security concerns, deterring shippers from entering the Gulf to load oil. In a sign of de-escalation, Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the vital strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. IG market analyst Tony Sycamore says, “The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the Strait, potentially through an attack on a U.S. base or a tanker transiting the waterway.” Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend while traffic in the Strait of Hormuz slowed following reports of vessel attacks, shipping data showed on Monday. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday. On Sunday, Opec+ approved an oil production quota increase of around 188,000 barrels per day from September, the producer group said, in a move that completes the unwinding of a layer of voluntary output cuts. Due to export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstan caused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, successive monthly Opec+ hikes over most of this year have remained largely on paper with little impact on the market.

Bulls in charge as PSX opens week by gaining 2,000 points during intraday trade. The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) opened the week in the green, gaining more than 2,000 points during intraday trade. At 11am, the benchmark KSE-100 index had gained 2273.78 points, from the previous close of 176,094.11 points. The development came as global oil prices tumbled on Monday as Donald Trump said fresh talks with Iran will begin later in the day. Mettis Global, a web-based financial portal, said the positive momentum at PSX came as “investors took cues from easing geopolitical tensions after Trump called off a planned strike on Iran, reducing immediate concerns over a wider regional conflict”. Awais Ashraf, director of research at AKD Securities, said investor optimism extended the positive momentum from the previous week, driven by expectations of a swift agreement between the US and Iran. “Sentiment improved after the US president announced that talks with Iran would resume on Monday, without setting a deadline for reaching an agreement following the cessation of hostilities,” he said. Ashraf added that “the return of inflation to single digits in July, with the data due to be released today, would provide an additional catalyst for the market by strengthening expectations of monetary easing and further boosting investor confidence”. The KSE-100 index ended the first month of the current fiscal year lower. According to Topline Securities Ltd, the index closed July down 4,208 points or 2.3 per cent month-on-month as escalating US-Iran tensions pushed global crude oil prices higher, weighing on investor sentiment. Average daily traded volume during the month stood at 845 million shares, while average daily traded value was Rs37.5bn. Additional input from AFP

PML-N bags 14 seats in 2nd phase of AJK polls amid allegations of rigging. The PML-N has bagged 14 seats while the PPP has managed to secure just four of the total 18 seats that were up for grabs in the second phase of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) election on Sunday, according to unofficial results released by the Election Commission. Polling was postponed until Tuesday in LA-27 Muzaffarabad-I (Kutla) and at 71 of the 174 polling stations in LA-28 Muzaffarabad-II (Lachhrat) as polling staff and election material could not reach the constituency because of landslides and bad weather that resulted in blocked roads. State broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported the unofficial results of 18 seats, citing Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal’s press talk in Muzaffarabad. During the press talk, he announced that the PML-N had won 14 seats and the PPP four. Unofficial results LA-34 bagged by PML-N’s Nasir Dar LA-35 bagged by PML-N’s Chaudhry Muhammad Ismail LA-36 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Ahsan Raza LA-37 bagged by PNL-N’s Maryam Javed LA-38 bagged by PML-N’s Zeeshah Ali LA-39 bagged by PML-N’s Raja Muhammad Siddique Khan LA-41 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Amir Shah LA-42 bagged by PML-N’s Syed Shawkat Ali Shah LA-43 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Yasin Lone LA-44 bagged by PML-N’s Ahmad Raza Qadiri LA-25 bagged by PML-N’s Ghulam Qadir LA-30 bagged by PML-N’s Mustafa Bashir Abbasi LA-31 bagged by PML-N’s Saqib Majeed Khan LA-32 bagged by PML-N’s Raja Farooq Haider Khan LA-40 bagged by PPP’s Amir Abdul Ghaffar Khan LA-45 bagged by PPP’s Abdul Majid Khan LA-26 bagged by PPP’s Mian Abdul Waheed Khan LA-29 bagged by PPP’s Sardar Mukhtar Ahmad Khan On Sunday, the PPP accused the PML-N — its ally in the Centre — of electoral malpractices, rigging and violence, as it had during the first phase of the elections in Mirpur division on July 27. PML-N secured nine of the 13 seats in the first phase while the PPP won the remaining four. Polls in AJK are being held in three phases over security concerns, with the polling held on seven seats of Muzaffarabad division and 12 refugee seats, the reserved seats for refugees from India-occupied Kashmir. In the third phase, polling will be held in 11 constituencies of Poonch division. PML-N now has ‘govt-forming number’: Rana Sana As the unofficial results were released, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs and PML-N leader Rana Sanaullah said his party had now gained the “simple majority” needed to form a government in AJK. He was addressing a press conference alongside Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam. “We have the government-forming number,” he said, adding that “there are a total of 45 seats […] and out of 45, PMLN has so far secured 23 seats”. The PML-N leader said his party had won in four of the seven territorial constituencies in Muzaffarabad while the PPP, which had been “attempting to build a rigging narrative since 10:30am yesterday”, had secured three. Sanaullah demanded that the PPP must tell the people how they managed to secure three seats despite the alleged rigging. “Did they succeed because of rigging or because of a free and fair election?” Sanaullah further stated that the PML-N had also secured 10 out of 12 refugee seats while the PPP had won two. “A democratic government, which has the people’s mandate, will now be formed in AJK, and it will work on ideological, economic, and political affairs of the region,” he said. He added that a parliamentary party session of the PML-N would be called after the conclusion of the third phase of the elections for future decisions. Speaking about PPP’s rigging allegations, the PML-N leader dismissed them and accused PPP of colluding with the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) to disrupt the election process in Muzaffarabad. “Anticipating PML-N’s win, PPP along with the action committee planned riots and [..] fired at the police personnel when they got there,” Sanaullah alleged. He claimed that the incident created an atmosphere of fear in the area, which led to a lower turnout. “We received at least 3,000 to 4,000 fewer votes due to this,” he claimed. On PPP’s allegations that an attempt had been made on its candidate AJK Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar’s life, he accused the party of staging a “drama”. He also claimed that the PPP had refused to get Akbar’s medicolegal examination done. Sanaullah accused the PPP of employing “dirty tricks” to sabotage the electoral process, saying that the PPP’s actions violated the Charter of Democracy, in which the party leadership had agreed that they would not “malign each other’s mandate with such dirty tricks”. Reports of violence During the polling on Sunday, attempts were reportedly made to disrupt polling in some neighbourhoods of Muzaffarabad, but voting continued in most areas. In LA-31, Muzaffa­rabad-V (Khawra), clashes between workers of the PML-N and PPP were reported in Union Council Katkair. The PPP alleged that one of its workers, Syed Mushtaq Shah, was killed in an attack by PML-N supporters. The PML-N rejected the allegation, claiming the man suffered a cardiac arrest following a scuffle between two groups. There was no independent confirmation of either claim. PPP candidate and Legislative Assembly Speaker Akbar also wrote to the AJK chief election commissioner, alleging security lapses, firing incidents, interference in polling, prevention of polling agents from entering polling stations and denial of voting rights. He also claimed there had been an attempt on his life in which Advocate Syed Mumtaz Hussain Naqvi was injured, and called for an investigation and legal action against those responsible. There was no immediate response from the Election Commission. Clashes between workers of the two major parties, some involving the use of firearms, were also reported from other areas, though no casualties were immediately reported. Low turnout outside AJK Outside AJK, Kashmiris voted for their candidates vying for refugee seats at polling stations set up in Chakwal, Jhelum, Rawalpindi, Islamabad, Sialkot, Narowal, Sargodha, Attock, Nawabshah, Hyderabad, Mohmand, Mansehra, Quetta, Dera Ghazi Khan, Peshawar, Sanghar, and Naushahro Feroze. Polling in these areas largely remained peaceful and recorded a low turnout. In Mohmand, not a single voter turned up at a station set up for the AJK polls. In Dera Ghazi Khan, a single registered female voter cast her ballot at the Govt Elementary School in Maumori, where a polling station had been established just for her. Out of 12 refugee seats, seven seats are in Punjab, one seat is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, one seat (Jammu-VI) is divided between Pun­jab, Islamabad, and Khyber Pakhtun­khwa, one seat is divided between Sindh and Balo­chistan (Valley-I), and one seat (Jammu-I) is shared among refugees living in Balochistan, Punjab, and Sindh. Valley-V seat is divided between Punjab and Islamabad. Since early June, AJK has witnessed protests by the now-proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding the abolition of the 12 refugee seats in the AJK legislature. The protests have also been marred by violence .

Granted a singles wild-card entry at the WTA 1000 event, the 46-year-old Williams has lost 12 straight matches dating to July 2025. “We play outside … you can’t control the weather,” Williams said. “But the fans were amazing. She's ranked 82nd in the world. “Playing Venus is not an everyday experience,” Rakhimova said. “I’m very glad to actually get a chance to play against her. I was looking forward to that match. I knew it was going to be a center-court match. I was trying to enjoy my time on it, no matter what the result."

Aboitiz unit starts construction on 239-megawatt Negros solar facility. Aboitiz Renewables Inc. began construction of its 239-megawatt solar project in Negros Occidental, expanding its clean energy capacity in the region as local governments seek to diversify the national power mix. The renewable energy unit of Aboitiz Power Corp. said on Monday, Aug. 3, that it will build the Luna Solar Power Plant in Barangay Luna, Cadiz City, alongside an integrated 65-megawatt battery energy storage system. Full commercial operations are targeted for 2028. The facility is the company’s first combined renewable generation and battery storage site on Negros Island and will be its largest solar installation in the Visayas region. The added capacity will raise the company’s solar portfolio in the region by 471 megawatts. Aboitiz Renewables already operates two clean energy assets in the province: the 173-megawatt Calatrava Solar Power Plant and the 59-megawatt SacaSun facility in San Carlos City. The decision to build a third and larger installation reflects strong natural solar potential and local policies that streamline clean power development, Aboitiz Renewables President Jimmy A. Villaroman said. National policymakers have pushed to broaden the Philippine energy mix, pointing to host communities with high solar irradiance as crucial to expanding green capacity. Local government officials welcomed the multi-million-peso facility, citing economic development opportunities and new industrial activity. Cadiz City Mayor Salvador Escalante Jr. said hosting the project demonstrates the city's ability to attract large industrial ventures beyond its traditional agricultural foundation. The investment reinforces Negros Occidental’s standing as a clean energy hub, supported by clear provincial regulations and reliable solar exposure. Adding the Luna facility brings Aboitiz Renewables’ total operating assets to 45 nationwide across solar, hydro, geothermal, and energy storage technologies. The company holds an additional development pipeline of more than 1,800 megawatts in prospective solar, wind, and hydroelectric projects. (Gabriell Christel Galang)

PDEA gets 1st Central Visayas drug-linked money laundering conviction. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) has secured a very first conviction of a locally initiated money laundering case relating to illegal drugs activities in Central Visayas. In a statement on Monday, Aug. 3, PDEA said that Marie-Den Sarol Barbecho was found guilty beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Sections 4(a) and 4(b) of Republic Act No. 10365 or The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001. Barbecho was sentenced to one year imprisonment and a fine of P500,000. The case stemmed from money laundering cases filed on February 2023 by PDEA Regional Office VII, following a financial investigation arising from the Agency’s anti-illegal drug operations against Barbecho. Barbecho, who has no known gainful source of income or commensurate financial capacity, transacted money in different amount and to different recipients amounting to a total of ₱1,739,551.00. The April 27 decision handed down by the Cebu City Regional trial Court Branch 11 marked the significant milestone in PDEA’s campaign against illegal drugs and the financial networks that support them, according to PDEA Director General Isagani R Nerez. Nerez said the agency reaffirms its commitment to strengthening financial investigations and working closely with its partner agencies to dismantle drug trafficking networks, seize illicit assets, and ensure that those who profit from the illegal drug trade face the full force of the law.

Toni Fowler on removing her breast implants: 'Araw-araw ang bigat ng dala ko'. Content creator Toni Fowler, who is also known as Mommy Oni, took a major step recently, deciding to remove her breast implants after 10 years. In her recent vlog, Toni showed the journey of her surgery and recovery, giving her followers an honest glimpse into why she ultimately felt it was time to part ways with the implants that had become a defining part of her image throughout her years as a content creator. According to Toni, she did not have her breast implants removed back in May—even though they were due for replacement—because she wanted to first celebrate their "ten years of relevance" in her career as a content creator. "Inuna ko muna 'yung ten years of relevance na celebration ko with the ToRo family. Inuna ko muna 'yung mga trabaho ko, 'yung mga dapat kong tapusin, bago talaga ako magpa-opera," She said. Toni went through the surgery with the help of Celebrity plastic surgeon Doc Yappy. Having implants for the longest time, Toni admitted that she was always curious about what she would look like if she were flat-chested. "Buong buhay ko, hindi ko talaga na-experience ang maging flat kaya talagang naging fantasy ko talaga na maging flat. Ewan ko, eh kasi di ba, ganu’n naman ‘yung buhay, kung anong wala sa ‘yo ‘yun ‘yung gusto mong ma-experience. Gusto kong maging flat talaga," she added. She also spoke about the physical discomfort she had lived with over the years. "Kasi ang hirap na rin sa araw-araw ng buhay ko na palaging ang bigat-bigat ng dala ko...ang hirap...kaya it's about time na tanggalin na ang nagpapa-kuba kay Toni Fowler." Toni also gave a heartfelt shoutout to her partner, Vince Flores, who stayed by her side throughout the surgery and recovery, as well as her daughter, Tyronia, who helped care for her after she was discharged from the hospital. "Sobrang ma-swerte ko talaga sa mag-ama ko kasi binabantayan nila ako. Actually, tandem sila pero mas grabe 'yung sacrifice ni Vince. Halos wala na siyang tulog, pinapakain niya ako palagi, at syempre may sinusunod kaming oras ng gamot. Grabe talaga 'yung pag-aalaga niya sa akin mula noon hanggang ngayon," she said. Toni’s son, Tyrone, also stopped by later in the vlog to check on her as she recovered from surgery. After removing the gauge, Toni and Vince were both shocked upon seeing the result of the surgery. "Grabe sobrang gaan," Toni said, while Vince remarked, "Nakakapanibago." Embracing the change, Vince assured that his feelings towards Toni haven't changed. Meanwhile, Toni couldn't help but get emotional as she finally achieved her dream chest. "Nung nakita ko...sa salamin, parang bigla akong nalungkot. Pero masaya ako at the same time. Masaya ako kasi nagustuhan ko 'yung gawa sa akin...ang ganda niya, hindi na siya ganon kalaylay kasi nga nagka-baby na ako," Toni said. She continued: "Nung gumilid na ako -- oo gusto kong maging flat pero parang naramdaman ko na hindi ako babae. Kasi diba all my life parang 'yun 'yung nagbubuo sa pagka-babae ko eh...so nung time na nakita ko na flat na siya...hindi ko na feel na parang mommy ako, na babae ako. Parang na-feel ko na 'hala, hindi ako babae'. May ganon pero alam kong emosyon ko lang 'to dahil nga groggy pa rin ako sa gamot, anesthesia, and nalilito pa rin ako kasi big change 'to sa katawan ko." In addition to having her implants removed, Toni also underwent breast reduction. She shared that she already had a fuller natural chest before getting implants, so she opted for a modest reduction to achieve the look she had always wanted. "Ang tagal kong pinangarap 'to," she said.

Palestine turns to music as bridge for dialogue and cultural diplomacy. The Embassy of the State of Palestine transformed Manila’s Metropolitan Theater into a venue for cultural diplomacy as it hosted the Palestine–Philippines Music Concert on June 29, bringing together diplomats, government officials, artists, academics, and members of the public for an evening that explored themes of peace, justice, and human dignity through music. More than 450 guests attended the concert, including Secretary of Foreign Affairs Ma. Theresa P. Lazaro, Undersecretary Maria Theresa Dizon-De Vega, ambassadors and members of the diplomatic corps, senior government officials, representatives of international organizations, academics, students, and supporters of the Palestinian people. Rather than focusing on political discourse, the evening highlighted culture as a means of fostering dialogue and understanding between nations. The program opened with the national anthems of the Philippines and the State of Palestine before presenting five original compositions by Palestinian Ambassador Mounir Anastas, whose works explored universal themes of justice, memory, peace, and the dignity of human life. Among the featured pieces was “Requiem for Gaza”, an acousmatic composition that incorporates authentic sound recordings from Gaza as a tribute to innocent civilian victims of war. Other works included “Funeral Sentence”, a reflection on the death penalty; Reflection, written for two percussionists; “Small Étude for Peace”, expressing hope for a just and lasting peace; and “Motion of Confidence”, dedicated to the Filipino people in recognition of what Ambassador Anastas described as the Philippines’ commitment to international law, the protection of human rights, and its longstanding support for the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people. All five compositions were performed by leading Filipino musicians, underscoring the collaborative spirit of the concert. The second half of the program shifted the spotlight to Philippine musical heritage, with performances by acclaimed pianist Dr. Raul Sunico, percussionists Elizalde Tolentino and Aimee Dela Cruz, sopranos Elisanta Cortes and Thea Perez, and tenors Ronan Ferrer and Eugene De Los Santos. Their repertoire showcased Filipino classical and traditional compositions, reflecting the evening’s theme of cultural exchange. Welcoming guests, Ambassador Anastas thanked Secretary Lazaro for attending and formally dedicated “Motion of Confidence” to her and, through her, to the Filipino people. He also expressed his appreciation to the Filipino artists who brought his compositions to life. Speaking about “Requiem for Gaza”, the ambassador explained that the work transforms authentic recordings from Gaza into “a musical expression of remembrance, mourning, and hope.” He described music as a universal language capable of preserving memory, transcending borders, encouraging dialogue, and affirming shared values of justice, peace, freedom, and human dignity. The embassy said the concert forms part of its broader efforts to deepen cultural cooperation and strengthen people-to-people ties between Palestine and the Philippines, underscoring the role of the arts in fostering mutual understanding beyond traditional diplomacy.

Death toll from Kumamoto quake rises to 38. KUMAMOTO (Jiji Press) -- The death toll from Tuesday's powerful earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture, southwestern Japan, has risen to 38 as two more deaths have been confirmed, the prefectural disaster response headquarters said Sunday. A woman in her 70s died while sleeping in a car, apparently from heatstroke. Her death was judged potentially to be disaster-related, with the physical and mental strain of life as an evacuee among the possible causes. This is the first possible disaster-related death linked to the earthquake. The death toll includes other cases under investigation for suspected links to the disaster. With summer heat expected to intensify in areas hit by the disaster, the prefectural and central governments are rushing to prepare to help evacuees move to secondary evacuation facilities. As of Sunday afternoon, the number of damaged homes stood at 4,213. Water supply remained disrupted for 46,700 households. A total of 8,480 people were staying at 206 evacuation centers. But the number of people taking shelter in cars remains unknown. According to the prefectural disaster response headquarters, the woman was confirmed dead after she was found staying in the car on Thursday. The car's air conditioner was not working because the vehicle had run out of gas. Whether her death is officially recognized as disaster-related will be determined by a municipal examination board. In disaster-stricken areas in the prefecture, extreme heat with a maximum temperature of 35 degrees Celsius or higher continued after the earthquake, with authorities calling for caution against heatstroke. In order to prevent disaster-related deaths, the prefectural and central governments are working to secure secondary evacuation facilities. They are expected to be able to arrange accommodations for up to some 2,200 people at 73 facilities, such as hotels and "ryokan" Japanese-style inns, while considering how to transport elderly people and others to such places. The other newly confirmed fatality is a man in his 80s who was in the city of Uki in Kumamoto when the earthquake struck the prefecture. Recruitment of disaster volunteers has started in Uki, the city of Uto, the town of Misato and the town of Kosa, in addition to the towns of Mashiki, Kashima and Mifune. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, a total of 360 earthquakes measuring 1 or higher on the Japanese seismic intensity scale of up to 7 had occurred by 3 p.m. Sunday following Tuesday's temblor, including five quakes registering lower 5, the fifth-highest level, and 16 quakes registering 4.

Team Spirit rules MSC 2026; Team Falcons PH misses podium. For the first time ever, a team outside the Southeast Asian region has reigned supreme in an S-tier Mobile Legends: Bang Bang esports tournament. Team Spirit pulled off a nail-biting 4-3 victory over Yangon Galacticos of Myanmar to reign supreme in the 2026 Mid-Season Cup at the Esports World Cup in Paris, France over the weekend. The Eastern Europe Central Asia (EECA) Dragons raced to a commanding 3-1 lead in the series but still had to fend off a tough stand from Yangon Galacticos which did just enough to drag the contest to a winner-take-all Game 7. With the two teams engaging in a tug-of-war in the decider, Team Spirit gained the upperhand when jungler Zaur "zaur egoist" Magomadov secured the Lord to save his team from what could have been a miserable team fight after two of their heroes were nearly picked off by YG. Instead, the Lord push proved to be the difference as Team Spirit took down the base and won its first major title in MLBB esports. Team Spirit, the organization widely known for its success in Dota 2, ended a nine-year dominance of the SEA region or since teams from Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia ruled the MSC since its inception in 2017. Mathaios “Kid Bomba” Chatzilakos was named the Finals MVP, bagging $25,000 while the rest of the team which aside from Zaur Egoist, also included Kemiran “Sunset Lover” Kochkarov, Anton “Hiko” Pak and Stanislav “Sawo” Reshniak claimed the $1,000,000 top prize. Meanwhile, Team Falcons PH got swept by Indonesian rival Onic Esports, 3-0 led by Filipino imports Kairi “Kairi” Rayosdelsol and Duane “Kelra” Pillas in the battle for third. Onic Esports bagged $250,000 for finishing third while Team Falcons PH, the runners up of the MPL Philippines Season 17, settled for the fourth place with a $150,000 prize.

PWD killed in Lucena fire. LUCENA CITY, Quezon – A 21-year-old Person with Disability (PWD) was killed in a fire that destroyed his house in Purok 3-A, Bagong Sibol, Barangay Dalahican, this city, on Sunday morning, Aug. 2. The victim was identified as Jay Jay. Arson investigators said the fire which also razed five other houses started at 6 a.m. The fire was put out at about 7 a.m. The body of the victim was recovered in a mopping-up operation. Damage to property was placed at P100,000 and cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

Fire destroys 14 houses in Zamboanga City. ZAMBOANGA CITY – Fourteen houses were destroyed by a fire in Sitio Baliwasan Grande, Barangay Baliwasan, this city, on Sunday, Aug. 2. A total of 16 families were displaced by the blaze that broke out at around 2 p.m. Arson investigators are probing possible short circuit from a house as cause of the fire. Investigation added that neighbors extinguished an earlier fire and advised the homeowner to switch off the main circuit breaker to prevent another blaze. Hours later, the same wiring reportedly short circuited anew, igniting a second blaze which quickly spread to adjoining houses. The fire was put under control after nearly an hour. No casualties were reported and follow-up investigation is ongoing.

Chinese firm vows big upgrades for Holcim Philippines after buyout. China-based construction materials giant Huaxin Building Materials Ltd. has committed to continuous investment in one of the Philippines’ largest cement producers, following its takeover of the Holcim Group’s local unit in a deal worth over $800 million. Holcim Philippines Inc. President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Mohit Kapoor said in a statement that Huaxin is well-positioned to further develop the company over the long term, driven by its strong track record of delivering growth. “Holcim Philippines’ market position and long-term potential are promising, and Huaxin is committed to investing in its future growth as part of its international strategy,” said Kapoor. “Huaxin brings with it industrial technology, technical talent, and concrete plans to further grow the existing platform in the Philippines,” he added. Switzerland-based Holcim announced on Sunday, Aug. 3, that it had signed an agreement with Huaxin to transfer its shares in a deal valued at approximately $807 million (roughly ₱49.23 billion). The company will initially sell a 67.623-percent stake for $527 million, with its remaining 31-percent stake to be sold within the next three to five years for at least $280 million. Holcim noted that the transaction value may increase “based on incremental value creation during this period.” The deal remains subject to customary and regulatory approvals—including clearance from the Philippine Competition Commission (PCC)—with the sale of the majority stake expected to close in the first half of 2027. “We are excited about the opportunities ahead and remain focused on continuously delivering performance and value for all our stakeholders,” Kapoor said. Holcim Philippines operates four cement clinker plants, one cement grinding station, five ports, and multiple storage and distribution points nationwide. It has an annual clinker production capacity of 5.2 million metric tons (MT) and an annual cement production capacity of 9 million MT. In a regulatory disclosure, Huaxin stated that it plans to deploy its mature management systems and advanced production processes to boost Holcim Philippines’ capacity utilization. “The company has established a track record in successfully integrating and developing acquired companies, achieving post-acquisition performance improvements, and realizing targeted returns on overseas investments,” Huaxin said. With this acquisition, the Wuhan-based company adds another international firm to bolster its global presence, offsetting declining domestic demand. Huaxin currently operates across 14 countries, with an annual clinker output capacity of 26.60 million MT and an annual cement production capacity of 36.15 million MT. “This acquisition will further strengthen the group's business presence in Southeast Asia, expand its global production capacity, and enhance its international market influence and resilience against cyclical fluctuations,” the company added. Holcim Philippines voluntarily delisted from the Philippine Stock Exchange in 2023 after its public float fell below the minimum requirement following an equity purchase by its largest stakeholder, Holderfin B.V.

Cops arrest 473 people for illegal fishing, logging in Western Visayas; 182 more drug suspects fall. Police arrested a total of 473 people for illegal fishing and illegal logging as authorities intensified the campaign in implementing environmental laws in Western Visayas. Police Brig. Gen. Randulf T. Tuaño, director of the Police Regional Office 6, said the operations conducted in July also led to the confiscation of fish valued at ₱422,660.00, along with fishing equipment, motorboats, and other paraphernalia worth ₱31,018,540.00. The same operations also resulted in the confiscation of lumber worth ₱1,047,534.96 and charcoal valued at ₱125,180.00. “These operations were intended to protect the region's environment while supporting communities that depend on its natural resources for their livelihood. These also showed that protecting our environment is a shared responsibility,” said Tuaño. “Our police officers will continue to work closely with partner agencies and local communities to ensure that our forests, rivers, and coastal waters are preserved for future generations. We will remain consistent in enforcing the law while treating everyone with fairness and respect,” he added. The official also urged the public to remain vigilant and actively support environmental protection efforts by reporting illegal activities affecting forests, rivers, and coastal areas through the nearest police station or appropriate government authorities. He explained that timely information from the public helps the police respond more effectively and allows them to prevent further damage to the environment. On illegal drugs operations, Tuaño said they arrested 182 persons and confiscated almost P50 million worth of illegal drugs in the same month across the region. Among those seized were 7,321.29 grams of suspected shabu and 61.30 grams of suspected marijuana. Those arrested include 63 High-Value Individuals (HVIs), 109 Street-Level Individuals (SLIs), and one Drug Personality of Interest (DPOI). "Every drug seizure represents fewer illegal substances reaching our communities. Our goal is straightforward—to disrupt the illegal drug supply, protect our communities, and ensure that every police operation is carried out professionally and in accordance with the law,” said Tuaño. “These results remind us that consistent enforcement and public cooperation remain our strongest tools against illegal drugs," he added.

Jobert Sucaldito's son Carlo Brian breaks silence on his father's death. After the sudden death of veteran entertainment columnist Jobert Sucaldito on Sunday, his son, Carlo Brian, revealed what happened in the days leading up to his father's passing. In a Facebook post, Carlo shared that his father died from cardiac arrest and is currently lying in state at Loyola Memorial Chapels & Crematorium in Commonwealth. "Sadly, Nanay Jobert passed away yesterday due to cardiac arrest (heart failure), as explained by the doctors at the Philippine Heart Center. During the incident, he suddenly collapsed and fell, causing him to hit his head, which resulted in the bruise on his forehead and the cut on his lips. "His wake is currently being held at Loyola Memorial Chapels & Crematorium in Commonwealth, and everyone who wants to visit is welcome anytime until August 6, 2026," Carlo wrote. Carlo went on to reveal what happened to his father in the days leading up to his death. "A few weeks ago, Nanay was rushed to Providence Hospital because he really wasn't in good condition. The doctors recommended that he be admitted to the ICU, but if you all know Nanay, alam niyo kung gaano siya katapang at katigas ang ulo, in the best way possible. He wanted to keep fighting and continue enjoying life, and he kept saying, 'Kaya ko!' at 'Okay ako!'" According to Carlo, he respected his father's decision and they went back home, where his father continued with his usual routine. He added that Jobert's health had been steadily declining over the past few weeks, prompting them to spend more quality time together. "The last two weeks we spent together became some of the most unforgettable moments of my life. We went on road trips, visited places he enjoyed, shared meals, laughed together, and simply spent quality father-and-son time. Looking back, we noticed that his body was slowly getting weaker, but he never complained and never wanted anyone to worry. He always made us believe that he was okay, even when he probably wasn't," Carlo wrote.

Japan aims to rebuild 2-5 nuclear reactors by 2040s. TOKYO (Jiji Press) -- The Japanese government has decided to revise its nuclear energy policy guidelines to include a target of rebuilding two to five nuclear power reactors by the 2040s. The decision was adopted at a meeting of relevant cabinet ministers held at the prime minister's office on Friday to prepare for a projected power supply shortage in the 2040s due to the decommissioning of aging nuclear reactors that have been in operation for 60 years. "We will move forward with policies to ensure investment in nuclear power plants," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said at the meeting, suggesting that the government will also promote programs to nurture human resources. Industry minister Ryosei Akazawa outlined plans to reduce the burden on local governments and advance surveys by revising the basic policy regarding the selection of final disposal sites for high-level radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. It is the first time that the government as a whole has set a target for rebuilding nuclear plants since the 2011 triple meltdown at Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings Inc.'s Fukushima No. 1 plant. In the new guidelines, the reconstruction of Fukushima Prefecture, northeastern Japan, and the decommissioning of the Fukushima No. 1 nuclear plant are regarded as the most important issues. The government also projected that the country will need to rebuild 11 to 14 reactors by the 2050s. In its basic energy program adopted at a cabinet meeting in February last year, the government clearly stated its policy of making "maximum use" of nuclear plants. It aims to raise the proportion of nuclear power in the country's power supply mix to about 20 pct in fiscal 2040.

Guiao calls Hodge ‘league’s dirtiest player’; Meralco takes ‘strong’ exception. Rain or Shine head coach Yeng Guiao did not mince words and branded Meralco forward Cliff Hodge as the “dirtiest player in the league” — a remark that the Bolts franchise has taken exception to in its own statement a day after the Elasto Painters’ 85-83 win. The comments of thee fiery ROS mentor came after Hodge and Elasto Painters star Adrian Nocum figured in a knee-to-knee collision after the former tried to draw an offensive foul on the latter’s attack at the 4:06 mark of the third quarter. Nocum was slow to get up and immediately clutched onto his knee after the collision.
